January · Week 1

Shape Engineers & Building 🏗️

January 1 – January 7, 2027 · Days 1–7

This week she builds towers, bridges, houses and forts. Each day you put the same question in front of her in a new shape: what makes a structure stand up, and what makes it fall down? She knocks most of it over, rebuilds it steadier, and runs that loop seven times.

This is also the first week of the year, so on Day 1 you seal the time capsule you open on Day 365, start the growth chart on the door frame, and hang the first of twelve handprints. Those three threads run to December, and the rest of the week runs on cardboard.

🧒 What Azlyn will learn
  • Structures need a base. Wide bottoms hold, narrow ones topple.
  • Shape names in use (circle, square, triangle), attached to the boxes and cups in her hands.
  • Trial and error as a method. Build, watch it fail, change one thing, build again.
  • Hand strength and control through stacking, taping and pressing.
  • That she can make a real thing that stays in the house and that you use.
👶 KRESTON THIS WEEK

Kreston is 6 months this week. He sits propped with his hands free for short stretches, mouths everything he can reach, and starts rocking on hands and knees by the end of the week. He turns 7 months on Tuesday the 5th.

🌍 Around the world Week 1 · read it on Day 1

Mongolia, the Arctic & the American Southwest 🏠

Houses come in shapes other than boxes. Mongolian families build round felt gers they pack up and move with the seasons. Inuit builders cut snow blocks and lay them in a spiral to close an igloo. In the American Southwest, builders shape adobe homes from mud brick that keeps the inside cool through the heat.

✨
Try it

Swap the square house for a round one. A blanket over a laundry basket makes a good ger. Ask Azlyn which shape feels stronger.

  • Why kneading dough calms a wound-up kid down

Did you know

Mongolian gers always face south, toward the sun.

Opening activity · 8:00–9:00 AM

Sorting the Build Box

You need: the recycling pile · 3 paper bags or empty boxes · masking tape.

  1. The recycling you emptied onto the table last night is today's building kit. Carry it to the living room, tip it into one pile in the middle of the floor, and sit down in it with her.
  2. Give her three bags and three words: boxes, tubes, cups. Let her sort. She will argue about the odd ones, so let the argument run.
  3. Ask which shape she thinks will hold the most weight. Do not answer. Tell her you will find out at 9:15 and leave the question hanging.

🎨 MAKE
The main event · 9:15–10:15 AM

The Tallest Tower That Stands

⏱️ 60 min🧰 4 items

You need: The sorted boxes, tubes and cups, 1 roll masking tape, 1 measuring tape or a length of string, 1 permanent marker

  1. Build a tower as tall as you can with no tape. Let her place every piece. Do not correct the wobbly ones.
  2. It will fall. Say what could we change? instead of that was too narrow, and wait for her answer even when it takes a while.
  3. Build again, this time widest boxes at the bottom. Ask her which is stronger and let her push it to find out.
  4. Measure the tallest one against her. Mark the height on the wall with a pencil and write TOWER, JAN 1 beside it.
  5. Now hand her the tape and let her build a third one however she likes. Leave her to discover what tape lets her get away with.
  6. Leave the best tower standing. She will come back to it at 4:15.

💡Knocking it down is the measurement, so let her do it. A tower that stays up tells her nothing about why the others fell.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

First Walk of the Year

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Bundle up and walk the route you will walk all year. Look at the trees today, bare and sleeping, all structure and no leaves, the same thing she has been stacking all morning. Stop under the biggest tree on the route and take one photograph from where you are standing. Three more come from this spot this year. Hand her a paper bag and one instruction: find one thing worth keeping. It goes in the capsule this afternoon, so tell her that now.

The Time Capsule

Morning was tall, loud and falling over. This afternoon you seal a box and put it away for a year.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 8 items

You need: 1 shoebox with a lid, Thick card, 2 sheets, Washable paint and a wide brush, 1 wet washcloth in a shallow bowl, 1 pencil, 1 permanent marker, 1 measuring tape, Packing tape, Today's walk treasure

  1. Paint her palm with the brush rather than dipping her hand. Press flat, count to three, lift straight up. Write January and 3 beside it.
  2. Do Kreston's on the same sheet while he is calm, washcloth already in your hand.
  3. Stand Azlyn against the door frame. Mark, date and write her name. Draw round her flat hand next to her mark. Do the adults too so she can see the whole row.
  4. Ask her four questions and write the answers word for word: favorite color, favorite food, favorite song, what she wants to do this year. Do not tidy her grammar. Her wrong words are the ones you will want to read next December.
  5. Let her draw the family. Whatever comes out goes in.
  6. Load the box: the drawing, her answers, the walk treasure, a photo. Photograph everything first. Boxes go missing, and the photos on your phone will still be there.
  7. Tape it shut, write OPEN DECEMBER 31, 2027 across the lid, and put it somewhere she can see and not reach.

💡Let her shake it once it is sealed. Tell her it stays shut for a year, and let her sit with how long a year sounds.

  • Mail a letter to Azlyn for her to open when she is five
Day 1 · For the grown-up The Tower and the Time Capsule · Friday, January 1
👶 Infant integration morning

Put a cushion behind Kreston and give him his own cardboard tube and one paper cup on the floor, well back from the tower and out of its fall line. He will bang, mouth and drop them, running the same investigation Azlyn is running with the tower. On the walk, wear him facing out. The street and the cold air on his cheeks are new to him. Name three things you pass out loud.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He goes on the growth chart too, lying down. Mark and date his length at the same door frame as everyone else. After that, give him the flattened box to lie on. At six months he will stay with the crackle and the give under his hands longer than he stays with a toy, and down there he is at floor level with Azlyn while she works.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Why writing down her exact words matters more than you'd think.

Azlyn is in the fastest language stretch of her life, adding words at a rate nobody in the house is counting. Her mistakes are evidence of rule-building. She says I goed outside because she has worked out that adding -ed makes a thing past tense, and she applies that rule to the verbs she knows. Linguists call it overregularization, and it marks sophisticated thinking. You do not need to correct her. Feed the right form back in your next sentence (you went outside? what did you see?) and she picks up the exception on her own timeline, months after you first notice the rule.

⚠️

Safety: Keep tape rolls, craft sticks and walk treasure out of Kreston's reach the moment you stop watching him. Build the tower away from where he is sitting. Azlyn can step back when a cardboard tower comes down and Kreston cannot move out of the way. Washable non-toxic paint only.

Opening activity · 8:00–9:00 AM

Choosing the Box

You need: the big box · masking tape · 1 permanent marker.

  1. The big box you stood in the living room last night is waiting for her. Let her climb in before anything else happens. She will do this anyway.
  2. Ask what it should be: house, store, boat, rocket. Write her answer on the side in marker. The decision is now fixed and it is hers.
  3. Give her the tape and let her mark where the door and the windows go. She decides now, and you cut along her marks at 9:15.

🎨 MAKE
The main event · 9:15–10:15 AM

The Box House

⏱️ 60 min🧰 5 items

You need: 1 large box, tall enough for her to sit up in, 1 craft knife or heavy scissors (adult only), 1 roll masking tape, 1 permanent marker, Offcut card and small boxes

  1. Cut the door where she taped it this morning, on three sides so it swings open. Do this yourself with her standing back, and say why she is standing back.
  2. Cut two windows where she taped. Follow her marks even when they are in daft places.
  3. Hand her the offcuts and the tape and let her build a roof. It will be crooked and it will hold.
  4. Give her the marker. Every surface, inside and out, is hers to draw on.
  5. Write a house number on the front and let her choose the number.
  6. Get in with her. Sit down on the floor inside it and let her show you round.

💡Cut less than you think. You can cut more later, and a box with three walls left standing survives the whole week. A box cut into flaps lasts an afternoon.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

The Shape Hunt

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Walk the street looking for the shapes she sorted yesterday. Windows are rectangles, drain covers are circles, road signs are triangles, gates are made of squares. Ask her to find you three circles before you turn back. Say so out loud when she finds one you didn't see.

Furnishing the Box House

She moves somebody in this afternoon. Small boxes, cups and tape turn into the furniture.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: The box house, 6–10 small boxes, cups and tubes, 1 roll masking tape, 1 scrap of fabric or an old dish towel, 1 permanent marker, Crayons or paint

  1. Ask what a house needs. Take her list at face value even when it is a bed, a cake and a dog.
  2. Make the bed first: one of the small boxes with the fabric folded into it. Let her decide where it goes.
  3. Turn a tall box on its end for a table, cups upside down for stools.
  4. Cut a rectangle of card and tape it inside as a picture. She draws whatever hangs in it.
  5. Make one thing from her list that you would not have thought of. Follow her design down to the parts you would fix.
  6. Move a doll or a teddy in. Give it a name and write the name on the door.
  7. Turn the big light off and give her the flashlight. The cardboard glows and she will not want to come out.

💡Resist tidying the furniture into sensible positions. A stool on the roof is a decision, and if you move it she will stop making decisions.

Day 2 · For the grown-up The Box House · Saturday, January 2
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 6 months. Sit him inside the box house on a folded blanket while Azlyn draws on the walls around him. The light and the sound both change in there, and he will turn his head hunting for the difference. Put him in the middle of her project instead of beside it. Keep the door flap propped open so you can see him the whole time.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

Give him one of the small furniture boxes to handle before you tape it down. At 6 months he passes objects hand to hand and turns them over to look at the other side, both new this month, so watch his hands. Let him keep one box for himself, out of the build.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

The cardboard box beats the expensive toy, and there's a reason.

A toy fire engine can be a fire engine. A box can be a fire engine, a house, a boat, a bed, and a hiding place, sometimes inside ten minutes. Researchers who study play call that open-endedness, and children play longer and talk more with materials that have not decided what they are. A box also fails on her. It collapses, tears and needs mending, and each of those is a problem she gets to solve with tape while the fire engine sits there working. Hand her the packaging instead of what came in it and you have handed her the better object.

⚠️

Safety: The craft knife is adult-only. Put it back out of reach between cuts, on a shelf and not the arm of the sofa. Check inside the box for staples before either child gets in. Never leave Kreston in the box house alone, and keep the door flap open the whole time he is in it.

Save every cardboard tube in the house and put them by the stairs with the masking tape and a bag of dried beans.

🌅 START
Opening activity · 8:00–9:00 AM

Taping the Tubes

You need: cardboard tubes · masking tape · scissors · a smooth wall or the side of a closet.

  1. Fetch the cardboard tubes you piled by the stairs last night and cut two or three in half lengthways so they become open channels. You cut, she holds.
  2. Tape one channel to the wall at a slope. Roll a dried bean down it and watch where it lands.
  3. Ask her where the next one should go so the bean keeps traveling. Tape it exactly where she says, even if it will not work.
The Big Book of Little Days · January · Week 1Day 3 · morning →
Day 3 · The main event Ramps and Bridges · Sunday, January 3
⏱️ 9:15 onward
🎨 MAKE
The main event · 9:15–10:15 AM

The Ball Run

⏱️ 60 min🧰 5 items

You need: 6–10 cardboard tubes, some cut open, 1 roll masking tape, Dried beans, dried pasta, a ping-pong ball if you have one, 1 shallow box or saucepan for the bottom, A wall or closet side you don't mind taping

  1. The run grows on the wall where you taped the first channel this morning. Put the catching box on the floor at the bottom of that wall. You aim the whole run at that box.
  2. Work upward. She chooses each next position, you tape it. Narrate as you go: I'm taping this one steeper, let's see.
  3. Send one bean down the whole run after each piece you add.
  4. It will fail somewhere. Look at where the bean stopped, change that one joint and nothing else, then test again.
  5. Once beans run the whole way, try pasta, then the ball. Each weight runs the course in its own way, and she will spot that before you say anything.
  6. Leave it taped up. You take it down tomorrow as part of the demolition.

💡Hand her the words. This end is higher than that end teaches more here than is this end higher or lower?, and it keeps her building.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

Stick Bridges

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Find a puddle, a gutter or a gap between two stones and build a bridge across it with sticks. Test each one with a pebble. Most of them fall in. Ask her what a longer stick does, then what two sticks laid side by side do. The gloves come home wet.

🎨 MAKE
Second main event · 1:00–2:30 PM

The Bridge That Holds Teddy

The bridge goes between two chairs and has to hold a teddy while the gap keeps growing. Cardboard gets strong once she changes its shape.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: 2 dining chairs, set a hand's width apart to start, Flattened cardboard, several pieces, Craft sticks and cardboard tubes, 1 roll masking tape, 1 teddy or doll, A can of beans as the heavy test weight

  1. Set the chairs close together. Lay one flat piece of card between them and stand teddy on it. It holds.
  2. Move the chairs a hand's width apart and try again. Keep going until it sags.
  3. Ask what could we change? and wait. Odds are she says a bigger piece of card. Try it, and watch it sag again.
  4. Show her one trick and then step back: fold the card into a concertina, or roll it into tubes and lay them side by side. Let her work out which way up it goes.
  5. Test with teddy, then the can of beans, then both at once.
  6. Push the chairs as far apart as the bridge will survive and mark the floor with tape.
  7. Take a photo of the winning bridge with teddy standing on it.

💡When she gets stuck, count to five in your head before you help. Most of the time she starts again on her own inside those five seconds, and the fix she finds is worth more than yours.

Day 3 · For the grown-up Ramps and Bridges · Sunday, January 3
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 6 months and tracks moving objects across his whole field of view now. Sit him well back from the run, out of reach of the catching box, and drop a bean down while he watches from there. Do it four or five times, and the bean travels back up in your closed hand and never into his. He loses it at the top and finds it again at the bottom, which is early object permanence work, and it costs you nothing but pointing him in the right direction.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

Lay him under the finished bridge and let him look up through it. At 6 months he pushes up onto his forearms and leans after what he wants, so set the teddy a little past his reach on the far side of the bridge. He gets his shoulders round before anything else moves.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Narrating beats quizzing, every time.

You already narrate half the morning without noticing you are doing it. The pull is to turn the rest into a quiz (what color is that? how many? is it big or small?), because her answers feel like proof that she learned something, and you end up with a three-year-old performing for an adult. Give her the running commentary instead and she gets new vocabulary in a real context, sentence structures she has not built yet, and no pressure to be right. Parents who narrate hand their children more words to hear, and a wider range of them. Save your questions for the ones you cannot answer yourself, like what could we change? over a bridge that keeps sagging.

⚠️

Safety: Dried beans and pasta are a choking hazard and they will end up on the floor. Sweep before you put Kreston down, and keep the catching box off the floor when he is loose in the room. Scissors stay with you.

TONIGHT, 9 PM
Prep for Day 4

Mix the salt dough for Tuesday: 2 cups flour, 1 cup salt, 1 cup water. Bag it and leave it in the fridge, and put out a clean sock and a ball of string for tomorrow.

Opening activity · 8:00–9:00 AM

Cup Pyramids

You need: paper cups, 20 or so · a flat bit of floor.

  1. Build a pyramid together: six cups along the bottom, then five, then four.
  2. Take one cup out of the bottom row and see what happens. Then put it back and take one from the top instead.
  3. Ask which cup is doing the most work. Take her answer as it comes and tell her you will test it for real at 9:15.

Day 4 · The main event Demolition Day · Monday, January 4
⏱️ 9:15 onward
🎨 MAKE
The main event · 9:15–10:15 AM

The Knock-Down Experiment

⏱️ 60 min🧰 4 items

You need: Boxes, cups and tubes from the build box, 1 roll masking tape, Paper and a marker for recording, The ball run from yesterday, still taped to the wall

  1. Build three towers side by side, all the same height. Tower one has a wide base. Tower two is a straight stack. Tower three is widest at the top on purpose.
  2. Give each one a number and write the numbers on paper.
  3. Push the floor near tower one with a flat hand. Count how many pushes before it goes. Write the number down. Repeat for two and three.
  4. Ask her which fell first and which held longest, and write her explanation word for word next to the numbers.
  5. Rebuild the winner and let her push it over herself, as hard as she likes.
  6. Now take down the ball run together and add its tubes to the pile.

💡Do not save the towers. You need them to fall to get the count, and the moment you ask her to be careful with one, she stops testing it.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

Stone Stacking

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Find flat stones and stack them as high as they will go on a wall, a step or a tree stump. She learned the wide-base rule indoors and will use it out here before you mention it. Leave the stack standing for the next person and walk past it tomorrow to see whether it survived.

🎨 MAKE
Second main event · 1:00–2:30 PM

The Wrecking Ball

This morning she knocked the towers over with her own hands. This afternoon she pulls a weight back, lets go, and the swing does the work for her.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: 1 clean sock, Dried beans or rice to fill it, 1 ball of string, about six feet, A door frame, and nothing else that could come down on her, All the boxes and cups, Masking tape

  1. Fill the sock a third full, knot it, and tie the string tight around the knot.
  2. Hang the free end from the door frame so the sock swings a hand's width above the floor.
  3. Build a tower right under the swing. Pull the sock back and let go. Do not throw it.
  4. Rebuild in the same spot and try releasing from lower down. Ask her which knocked more over.
  5. Move the tower further away and let her work out where the swing stops reaching.
  6. Let her build a tower she thinks can survive it. Test it. Let her be right or wrong without commentary.
  7. Finish by building one tower together that you both agree is too good to knock down, then knock it down anyway.

💡She will want to swing the sock by hand. Let her, once, then go back to releasing it. The height she starts it from decides how much falls over, and she sees that when she lets go instead of pushing.

The Big Book of Little Days · January · Week 1Day 4 · afternoon →

✨ Afternoon alternatives
  • Roll a ball at the towers instead of swinging anything.
  • Knock towers over with a cardboard tube used as a bat.
  • Build and flatten with feet only, no hands.
  • Stack cushions and jump into them.
🌳 Out again · pick one
  • The riverside path, to look at what holds the bank up
  • The woods loop, hunting for fallen trees and what pulled them down
  • The neighborhood park
  • The duck pond, and the bridge over it
  • Indoor playground, if it is pouring and nobody can face the coats
Day 4 · For the grown-up Demolition Day · Monday, January 4
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 6 months. Build him a two-cup tower within arm's reach and let him swipe it down. He will do it again and again without tiring of it, the same experiment Azlyn is running with three towers and a sheet of paper. Keep his cups separate from hers so nothing chewed goes back in the build box.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

Keep him well clear of the swinging sock. Put him in the far corner with the flattened box he liked on Friday. Once the wrecking is over, lie him on his back and swing a soft toy above him at a slow, steady pace. At 6 months he tracks a pendulum in one smooth sweep and stays with it longer than you would guess.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Knocking it down is the science.

You watch her flatten something she spent a solid fifteen minutes making, and it looks like fifteen minutes thrown out. She made a prediction while she built it, and knocking it down is how she collects the answer, so the demolition carries as much of the learning as the stacking did. Children work out the physical rules of the world by breaking things and watching how they break, which is why the same tower goes up and down eleven times. Say don't, you worked so hard on that and you save the cardboard while ending the experiment. Take a photo if you want the tower kept, then let her flatten it.

⚠️

Safety: Tie the string to something that cannot come down on top of her: a door frame, not a curtain pole or a shelf. Take the sock down and put the string away the moment you finish. A hanging loop of string is a strangulation risk, so do not leave it up overnight or within reach of either child.

Rolling the Bricks

You need: the salt dough · a rolling pin · a table knife · a floured board.

  1. The salt dough you left out overnight is this morning's clay. Give her a fist-sized lump and let her squash it for a few minutes before anything useful happens.
  2. Let her roll it out to about a finger's thickness and leave the uneven patches where they are.
  3. Cut rough rectangles with the table knife. They do not need to match. Aim for thirty and stop when she stops.

The main event · 9:15–10:15 AM

Salt Dough Bricks

⏱️ 60 min🧰 5 items

You need: The salt dough, 2 cups flour to 1 cup salt to 1 cup water, 1 rolling pin, 1 table knife, 2 baking trays and parchment paper, and a third cold tray for cooling, Extra flour for the board, 1 pencil for scoring

  1. Lay the bricks she cut this morning across both lined trays without touching each other.
  2. Let her press a mark into each one with her thumb, or scratch a line with the pencil. She owns the ones she marks.
  3. Set them in the oven at its lowest setting. They need two to three hours, so put them in now and take them out around lunch.
  4. While they bake, knead the leftover dough together. Give her a big lump, take one yourself, and sit with it. Ten minutes of quiet kneading does more for a wound-up morning than any instruction.
  5. Make three or four larger pieces (a doorstep, an arch, a chimney) and add them to a second tray.
  6. When they come out, spread them on a cold tray and leave them until 1:00, because warm bricks crumble.

💡They will not all survive. Bake ten more than you need and hand the broken ones back to her as rubble, which she will play with more than the whole ones.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

The Cold Walk

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Keep it short and brisk today, because the oven is on. Go past yesterday's stone stack first and see whether it survived. Look for frost on car roofs and in the shade at the bottom of walls. Let her breathe out and watch it. Find one brick wall and put her hand flat on it so she can feel how cold stone gets and see how many bricks it took.

🎨 MAKE
Second main event · 1:00–2:30 PM

Building the Brick Wall

The wall goes up on a tray, one row at a time. She lays every brick herself, and the thirty she cut are the whole supply.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: The cooled salt dough bricks, thirty or so, A flat tray or baking sheet as the building site, 1 small bowl of flour and water paste, 1 teaspoon for the paste, A ruler or a straight piece of card, The teddy from Sunday

  1. Lay a row of bricks in a straight line along the tray. Push them tight together.
  2. Build a second row straight on top with every joint matching. Push it and watch the whole wall hinge apart.
  3. Rebuild the second row offset, each brick bridging the gap below it. Push again. This one holds, and she will feel the difference in her hand.
  4. Keep going up. Use the paste between rows like mortar if the wall gets tall enough to need it.
  5. Leave a gap for a door and lay one long brick across the top of it. That is an arch, and it is holding up everything above it.
  6. Build a second wall at a right angle to the first so they lean on each other.
  7. Stand teddy inside. Photograph the wall next to the tower from Day 1.

💡Do not explain the offset in step three before she has seen the matched-joint wall fall apart. She needs the collapse first for the fix to mean anything.

  • Press leaves and buttons into the leftover dough instead.
  • Paint the dried bricks and build tomorrow.
  • Sort the bricks by size into rows and stop there.

  • Indoor playground if the pool is shut for the holidays

Day 5 · For the grown-up Bricks and Mortar · Tuesday, January 5
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston turns 7 months today. He reaches across his own body for something on the far side now, so press a spare lump of dough into a small rigid pot and tape the lid on hard, then set it a little past his midline for him to stretch toward. Check the tape every time and take the pot back the moment you stop watching. Salt dough is far too salty to be eaten. Say happy seven months out loud, because nobody else will.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He has swimming today too if he is coming. At 7 months he can sit supported in the water and splash with real intent. Keep it to twenty minutes and get him out before he is cold. Hold him chest to chest facing you for the first few minutes so the noise arrives with your face already in front of him.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Why kneading dough calms a wound-up kid down.

Push, squeeze and pull something that resists you, and you are doing what occupational therapists call heavy work, one of the steadiest ways to settle a small body. The pressure through her hands and joints feeds her proprioceptive sense, the one that tracks where her body is, and a kid who has lost track of it is the one climbing the back of the sofa. Dough costs pennies and pushes back for as long as she keeps working it. Ten minutes of it on a morning that has gone loud will settle her further than a talk about calming down.

⚠️

Safety: The oven is on for three hours today, so say it out loud when she comes near, and keep Kreston out of the kitchen while the trays move. Salt dough is dangerous if eaten, and seriously so for a 7-month-old and for any dog in the house. Count the bricks in and out and store them high. At the pool Kreston stays inside arm's reach in the water every second, and no float or seat stands in for your hands.

Craft Stick Shapes

You need: craft sticks · masking tape cut into short tabs.

  1. Tape four sticks into a square. Let her do the taping, however it comes out, with your thumb holding the corners.
  2. Tape three sticks into a triangle beside it.
  3. Press one finger on the top corner of each. The square folds flat and the triangle holds. Say nothing else about it and leave both on the table until 9:15.
Materials, laid out d6-materials.png

Day 6 · The main event Triangles Hold · Wednesday, January 6

🎨 MAKE
The main event · 9:15–10:15 AM

The Triangle Test

⏱️ 60 min🧰 5 items

You need: 30–40 craft sticks, 1 roll masking tape, The square and triangle from this morning, Cardboard tubes, 4 or 5, A small toy as the test load

  1. Hand her the folded square and ask her to make it stop folding. Then wait, and hold the silence a good while longer than feels comfortable.
  2. If she gets stuck, put one loose stick on the table beside it and say nothing more. Most children lay it across the diagonal within a minute.
  3. Once the square has a diagonal, push it together again. It holds now, because the diagonal turned it into two triangles.
  4. Build a tall tower out of taped triangles. Build a second out of taped squares. Race them upward.
  5. Load both with the toy and push both over. Write down which survived.
  6. Go and look at the box house from Saturday and find where a triangle would fix its saggy roof. Add one.

💡Sit on your hands today. Every joint you fix for her takes away the exact thing the activity exists to teach.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

The Stick Shelter

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Lean long sticks against a fence, a low branch or a wall to make a tent shape, then let go and see whether it stands. Push the top the way she pushed the one on the table. A triangle out here behaves the same as one indoors. Put a stone or a leaf inside for her to shelter, and come back tomorrow to see whether the wind took it.

The Zip Line

She has spent the week building things that push down. A zip line pulls, the opposite force and a new idea for her.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: 1 ball of string, 10 feet, 2 dining chairs, or a door handle and a chair, 1 paper cup, 1 cardboard tube cut into a short ring, Masking tape and scissors, Small toys, a spoon, a dried bean (cargo of different weights)

  1. Tie the string tight between the chair backs, one end higher than the other. She decides which end is higher.
  2. Tape the paper cup to the cardboard ring so the cup hangs underneath, then thread the string through the ring before you tie the second end.
  3. Load the cup with a small toy at the high end and let go.
  4. Once it stops halfway, ask what would make it keep going. Raise the high end and try again. Let her be the one who lifts it.
  5. Race two different weights down the same line, and have her call the winner out loud before she lets go.
  6. Slacken the string right off and try again so she sees a sagging line stop the cup dead.
  7. Send one thing down for each person in the house and let her decide who gets what.

💡Ask her to predict before each run. Let her be wrong out loud, then watch. She keeps more from that than from a right answer she kept in her head.

  • Post things down the banister instead.
  • Make a pulley by looping the string over a door handle and hauling a bag up.
  • Tape a string across the bath and float things along it.
🌳 Out again · pick one
  • The library (every two weeks, and the first visit of the year)
  • Indoor playground if the library is packed with the holiday crowd
  • The store, and let her carry one thing
  • The park on the way home

Day 6 · For the grown-up Triangles Hold · Wednesday, January 6
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 7 months, rocking on hands and knees and starting to pull himself forward. Lay the taped triangle tower on its side within his reach and let him post his fingers through the gaps. He is learning that a shape has an inside. His hand goes in, meets air, comes back out, and then he tries the next gap along.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

Take him to the library too and sit him in the board-book corner. At 7 months he will chew the books, which is what board books are built for. Pick one with high-contrast pages. Let Azlyn choose his and carry it to the desk herself.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

The pause before you help.

Azlyn wrestling with a joint that will not hold looks like a child who needs you. Most of the time she needs four more seconds. Adults step in fast, often before the frustration has arrived, and every early rescue teaches the same background lesson: hard things get solved by someone else. Count to five before you move. If she is still stuck, give her the smallest nudge you can, the loose stick set on the table beside her while your hands stay off the tape. You are protecting the willingness she will need next year to stay with a hard thing.

⚠️

Safety: Take the zip line down and put the string away the second you finish. String at toddler height is a strangulation risk, and a serious one. Loose craft sticks stay off the floor while Kreston is down. They splinter, and they fit down his throat. The cargo ends up on the floor every run, and a dried bean and a spoon are both choking hazards, so sweep the whole floor under the line before you put him down. He gets a taped structure too big for his mouth and nothing looser than that, and it comes back to you the moment you stop watching. The scissors stay with you.

The Blanket Fort

⏱️ 60 min🧰 6 items

You need: 3–4 blankets or sheets, 4 dining chairs, Sofa cushions, Clothespins or binder clips, Heavy books to weight the edges, The salt dough bricks from Tuesday

  1. Set the chairs on the corner marks you taped this morning, with their backs outward. That is the frame.
  2. Drape the first sheet across the top and clip it to the chair backs. Clips hold where tucked edges pull loose.

Living in the Fort

The whole afternoon happens inside the fort. She eats in there, reads in there, draws in there, and it stays up until bedtime.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 7 items

You need: The fort, 1 flashlight, A picnic blanket or towel for the floor, Snack and a drink in a lidded cup, 4–5 books, Paper and crayons, Your phone, for the week's photos

  1. Move in. Floor covering first, then the flashlight, then the books.
  2. Eat the afternoon snack inside. Food in a fort is most of the appeal.
  3. Turn the big light off and do shadow shapes on the roof (triangle, square, house).
  4. Read two books in there by flashlight, and let her hold it even though it will point at the ceiling the whole time.
  5. Look back through the week's photos together: the tower, the box house, the bridge with teddy on it, the brick wall. Ask which one she would build again.
  6. Let her draw the fort from the inside while she is inside it.
  7. Leave it standing overnight. Tomorrow you turn it into something else.

💡Go in with her, then stop directing. The hour has nothing to achieve, and she spends it in a small space she chose the shape of.

Day 7 · For the grown-up The Fort · Thursday, January 7
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 7 months and this is his best day of the week. Lay him on his back inside the fort and let him look up at the light through a sheet. Sit him against a cushion by the doorway so he can watch Azlyn come and go, which at this age is a game in itself. Keep the doorway open, keep cushions clear of his face, and stay in there with him.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

Take him into the store in the carrier facing out. At 7 months the noise, lights and strangers of a supermarket are work for him, so twenty minutes is plenty. Back home, put him in the fort doorway with one board book while Azlyn reads inside. He will hold it upside down and be pleased with it.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Why small enclosed spaces are so appealing right now.

Azlyn goes under the table, into the cupboard, behind the sofa. She hides in them, and she also uses them to shrink the world. A small space cuts how much arrives at once, and she cannot filter noise and light and movement yet, so walls close enough to touch give her relief. The fort is also the first territory she controls: she picked the shape, the door and who comes in. If she wants to be in there on her own, let her. Leave it up for a few days. A fort that survives to a second morning gets played in harder than one built fresh, because she starts from something she already owns.

⚠️

Safety: Nothing heavy on top of the fort and nothing that can fall inward. Books go on the outside edges, never on the roof. No cords, no holiday lights, no string left from yesterday. Never leave Kreston in there on his own, and keep pillows and loose blankets away from his face. The salt dough bricks stay off the floor and out of the doorway while he is in the fort. Salt dough is dangerous if eaten.

Day 8
Shakers and Spoons
The Big Book of Little Days · January · Week 1Day 7 · for the grown-up
January · Week 2

Nursery Rhymes & Rhythm 🎶

January 8 – January 14, 2027 · Days 8–14

Every rhyme she knows is a machine for keeping time, and this week she takes them apart. She fills five shakers and lines them up quietest to loudest, drops an egg off a wall she built herself, counts five ducks down to none and back again, and hits an upturned saucepan once for every piece of a word. The rhymes stay the same all week. Her job with them changes each morning.

No holiday lands in this stretch, so the week runs on its own thread and the gear piles up as it goes. Five sealed shakers on Friday, a kitchen drum kit on Monday, a hat and a flag on Thursday, and by the last afternoon the whole house is marching a route Azlyn drew on a sheet of paper on the floor. Three afternoons end with your phone recording her singing, one of them a song she writes about Kreston. Back those up before Thursday.

🧒 What Azlyn will learn
  • The beat inside a word. AZ-LYN is two hits, SPA-GHET-TI is four, and she hears the pieces long before she can name them.
  • Loud and quiet on purpose. Scarf up is loud, scarf down is quiet, and she is the one holding the scarf.
  • Counting down, and starting again from one. Five ducks to none, ten in the bed to one, five buns off a tray.
  • Calling it before it happens. She says cracked or not cracked out loud, then opens her hand over the tray and finds out.
  • Patterns she can hear. Spoon, cup, spoon, cup, and the gap where you took one out of the middle.
👶 KRESTON THIS WEEK

Kreston is 7 months this week. He reaches across his own body for something on the far side, moves a toy from one hand to the other to get a better look at it, and babbles in long strings with a beat running through them.

The Big Book of Little Days · JanuaryWeek 2 · opener →
🌍 Around the world Week 2 · read it on Day 8

Lullabies Everywhere 🌙

Every country puts its children to sleep with a song, and the songs resemble each other more than the languages do. Wales has Suo Gân, sung on the same slow fall as the Japanese Itsuki no Komoriuta. Swahili families sing Lala salama, sleep safe. Researchers played babies lullabies from cultures they had never heard, and the babies settled to those too.

✨
Try it

Warm milk with a cinnamon stick, the bedtime drink in a great many houses. Give Azlyn hers in the same cup all week and sing one lullaby that is not in English.

The Big Book of Little Days · JanuaryWeek 2 · around the world →
Around the world w2-world.png
👩 What you'll learn
  • Why she only has one volume, and it is loud
  • Why the rhymes she loves are all a bit gruesome
  • Why she wants the same rhyme forty times
  • Rhythm and reading are more connected than they look
  • Why a wind-down object works better than a wind-down instruction
  • Counting words come long before counting means anything
  • Why moving together matters more than moving
Did you know

Lullabies the world over share a slow, falling tune, which is why a song in a language she has never met still works on her.

Listening to the Cupboard

You need: the dry-goods cupboard, open · 1 metal spoon · 5 empty pots with lids.

  1. Sit her in front of the open cupboard and let her tap the packages with the back of the spoon. Rice, pasta, lentils, cereal, sugar. Each answers in a different voice.

  3. Line up the five pots and let her decide which package goes in which. You label them at 9:15.

The Shaker Set

⏱️ 60 min🧰 9 items

You need: 5 small plastic bottles or yogurt pots with lids, Dried rice, 1 cup, Dried lentils, 1 cup, Dried pasta shapes, 1 cup, Sugar, 2 tablespoons, Dry cereal, a handful, Packing tape, 1 permanent marker, 1 sheet of paper rolled into a funnel

  1. Roll the paper into a cone, tape the seam and stand it in the first pot. She pours, you hold. Some goes on the table and that is the price.
  2. Fill each pot a third full. A pot packed to the lid makes almost no sound, so let her overfill one and hear it.
  3. Tape every lid all the way round twice and press the seams flat. Write the contents on the side of each pot in marker.
  4. Shake them one at a time with her eyes shut. Ask her to point at the loudest before she opens them.
  5. Stand all five along the table, quietest to loudest. Move them as often as she wants.
  6. Number the bases one to five once she settles. She comes back to this line at 4:15.

💡The sugar shaker sounds like rain and she will lose interest inside a minute. Keep it. It is the quiet end of the line, and the only instrument in this afternoon's whisper verse.

🌳 OUTSIDE

Tapping the Railings

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Take a wooden spoon out with you and tap what you pass. Railings ring and hold the note, fence posts thud and stop dead, a trash can booms, a brick wall gives back nothing. January metal is cold enough that she will want gloves on and then off again to feel it. Let her find the loudest thing on the street and stay at it.

Loud Song, Quiet Song

The shakers have their order. This afternoon Azlyn plays one rhyme four ways and decides which way comes next.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 5 items

You need: The five sealed shakers, 1 saucepan and 1 wooden spoon, 1 cardboard tube for a megaphone, 1 scarf as the conductor's signal, Your phone, to record the last run

  1. Sit everyone in a ring, shakers in the middle, saucepan by your knee, scarf in Azlyn's hand.
  2. Pick a rhyme the whole house knows. Twinkle, Twinkle or The Wheels on the Bus. Sing it through once with a shaker each for you and Azlyn.
  3. Loud version. Saucepan on the beat, cardboard tube as a megaphone, pasta and lentils flat out. One verse, and one verse alone.
  4. Quiet version. Sugar shaker on its own, everyone whispering, heads close together. She drops her voice to match yours.
  5. Fast, then slow. Slow is the hard one, and one verse at half speed lasts longer than either of you expects.
  6. Hand her the scarf. Scarf up is loud, scarf down is quiet, and she runs the band. Follow her even when she flips it every two words.
  7. Record the last run. Play it back once, then again with everyone singing on top of it.

💡The whisper verse works better if you get smaller. Sit on the floor, lean in, let your voice go thin.

  • The neighborhood park, for twenty minutes of running
  • The bakery counter, and let her choose for tomorrow

Day 8 · For the grown-up Shakers and Spoons · Friday, January 8
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 7 months and reaching across his own body for things on the far side. Sit him back from the table with a wooden spoon and an upturned saucepan, and put the spoon down on his far side so he has to cross over for it. Keep the small pots away from him. Shake one by his left ear, then his right, and watch him turn toward a sound he cannot see.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He is 7 months and babbling in long strings now, ba-ba-ba and da-da-da-da, a rhythm section of his own. Sit him at the outside of the ring on your lap or with a folded blanket behind him, back from the shakers in the middle. He answers singing sooner than talking, so leave a gap at the end of each verse and see whether he fills it. Keep the loud verse short and watch his face while it runs.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Why she only has one volume, and it is loud.

Azlyn can do quiet on request and hold it for about four seconds. The holding is the hard part, and it runs on the same slow-growing machinery as waiting her turn and stopping halfway down the hall. Volume control is inhibition, and a three-year-old has a thin supply. She gets better at it by practicing the switch rather than by being asked for less noise. Handing her the loud verse first and the whisper verse second gives her both ends to feel in her own throat a minute apart. The scarf makes her the one calling the change, and running the switch builds it faster than obeying it.

⚠️

Safety: Dried rice, lentils and pasta on the floor are a choking hazard for a 7-month-old, and a taped lid can still come off. Tape all the way round each pot, check every seal before it goes down, and keep the small pots away from Kreston.

Drawing on the Eggs

  1. Fetch the four boiled eggs you left cold in the fridge last night, then hand her the marker and one egg at a time. Faces, hats, whatever she wants. Marker takes a minute to dry on a shell, so hold each one by the ends.
  2. Say the rhyme together while she draws. She will reach the line about nobody putting him together again and look up at you.
  3. Stand the best one in the egg cup on the windowsill. Nobody touches him before 9:15.

The Egg Drop Record

⏱️ 60 min🧰 7 items

You need: 4 hard-boiled eggs, boiled last night and cooled, or boiled at 8:00 and cooled fast in a bowl of cold water, 1 baking tray, 1 old towel to line the tray, 6–8 books or small boxes to build the wall, 1 permanent marker, Paper for the record, 1 tape measure

  1. Line the tray with the folded towel and set it on the kitchen floor. She stacks the books into a wall beside it.
  2. Sit Humpty on top and say the rhyme once with him up there.
  3. First drop from ankle height, straight into the tray. Measure with the tape and write the number down before she opens her hand.
  4. Ask her to call it before every drop: cracked or not cracked. Write her answer beside the number. Knee height next, then hip.
  5. Take the towel out for the last egg and drop it on the bare tray from ankle height. It breaks where it was safe five minutes ago.
  6. Read the paper back to her. Her numbers, her guesses, and the one that caught her out.

💡Let her hold the egg and let her be the one who opens her hand. An egg she drops herself is her experiment.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

The Low Wall Balance

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Find a low garden wall, a curb edge or the flat top of a step and walk her along it holding one hand. She sits at the far end with her legs over and says the rhyme from up there, then jumps into your hands. January stone keeps its frost all morning in the shade, so put your own hand flat on the top first.

The Mended Egg

Humpty's shell is still sitting on the tray. She glues him back together this afternoon, the one thing the rhyme insists nobody could do.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: The cracked shells from this morning, 1 sheet of thick paper or card, A glue stick, or flour and water paste in a saucer, 1 teaspoon for the paste, Crayons, 1 pencil to draw the egg outline

  1. Draw a big egg outline on the card in pencil, or let her draw it and go over her line so she can see it.
  2. Tip the shell onto a sheet of paper and let her press it small with the back of a spoon. Fingers work too.
  3. Mix the paste if you are using it: two tablespoons of flour, water stirred in until it runs like cream.
  4. Cover a small patch of the egg at a time. Paste the whole outline at once and it dries before she has filled a third of it.
  5. She presses the shell down. Let her go outside the line and leave gaps, and keep your hands off.
  6. Crayon in the rest: the wall underneath, the king's horses, a face on the shell.
  7. Write her title along the bottom in her own words, then put it up high to dry.

💡The shell runs out near the top and she will notice. Crayon fills the gap, and the picture is better for one bald patch.

Day 9 · For the grown-up Humpty Dumpty's Wall · Saturday, January 9
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 7 months and has started dropping food over the side of the high chair and leaning out to look. Same experiment, cheaper equipment. Sit him where he can see the tray for three or four drops. Then give him an egg cup on his own tray and pick it up eight times without comment.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

Keep him at the table and off the shells. Stick a long strip of masking tape to his high chair tray and let him work it loose. At 7 months he moves a thing from one hand to the other for a better angle. On the bus he wants the window, so face him out on your lap and name the stops.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Why the rhymes she loves are all a bit gruesome.

Humpty smashes. The cradle falls out of the tree, baby and all. Three mice lose their tails to a carving knife. Azlyn asks for these on repeat and then sleeps fine, because a rhyme keeps a small disaster inside a shape that never alters. She knows the ending before it arrives, so the fall frightens her the way a slide frightens her, with the floor already in view. Rehearsing an alarming thing at a safe distance is how she works out its real size. Dropping the egg herself went further again: she caused the crack, she stood over it, and it turned out smaller than the rhyme makes it sound.

⚠️

Safety: Shell fragments have sharp edges and are exactly the size Kreston puts in his mouth. Keep the tray and the glued sheet up high, sweep the floor before he goes down, and wipe egg off a hard floor straight away because it is slippery.

Making the Five Ducks

You need: 1 flattened cereal box · scissors (adult only) · crayons · 5 clothespins.

  1. Draw five duck shapes on the plain side of the box. Rough ovals with a beak on the front will do.
  2. You cut, she colors. Give each one something different, and let her choose which is the mother duck.
  3. Clip a clothespin to the bottom of each so they stand up. Line all five along the table and count them twice.

Over the Hill and Far Away

⏱️ 60 min🧰 7 items

You need: 1 cereal box, for cutting five duck shapes, Scissors (adult only), Crayons, 5 clothespins to stand the ducks up, 1 upturned laundry basket or a sofa cushion, 1 blue dish towel or scarf for the pond, Masking tape

  1. Turn the laundry basket upside down in the middle of the floor for the hill. Spread the dish towel in front of it for the pond and tape the corners flat.
  2. Stand all five ducks on the pond. Run a strip of masking tape across the floor behind the hill to mark where far away starts.
  3. Sing the first verse. On the line about only four coming back, she takes one duck over the hill and stands it on the tape.
  4. Count what is left on the pond after each verse, touching each duck as its number comes. She does the quacking, all of it.
  5. Keep going down to none, and sit in the quiet of an empty pond before the last verse.
  6. Mother duck calls and all five come back over together. She carries them, and she will want the whole thing again, so do it again.

💡Put the vanished ducks somewhere she can see the tops of. A duck gone for good gets checked on halfway through the next verse.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

Walking in a Duck Line

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Walk the block in single file. She goes first as the mother duck, everyone behind her waddles, and at each corner the person at the back moves to the front. Count off before you set out and count again at home to see whether anybody went over the hill and far away. January puddles have ice at the rim and she will stamp every one of them.

The Rhyme Bag

One object per rhyme goes into a pillowcase, and the bag decides what the house sings.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 3 items

You need: 1 pillowcase or tote bag, 6–8 household objects, one per rhyme: a spoon, a card star, a rolled sock, a watch, a plastic cup, an egg cup, one of the cardboard ducks, 1 sheet of card and 1 marker for picture labels

  1. Gather the objects and give each one its rhyme out loud. The spoon ran away with the dish, the mouse ran up the watch, the sock is Diddle Diddle Dumpling.
  2. Draw a picture label on card for each one, rough and fast, and lay it beside its object.
  3. Everything into the pillowcase. She reaches in without looking, feels about, pulls one out.
  4. Whatever comes out, the whole house sings it. No skipping and no swapping.
  5. Let her guess by feel before she looks, one guess out loud.
  6. Once the bag is empty, lay the objects in the order they arrived and sing the set through as one medley.
  7. Refill it and hand her the bag. She runs it and you sing whatever she pulls.

💡Slip in one object with no rhyme attached, a shoe or an apple, and let her invent something when it comes out. Her version goes in the bag with the rest.

Day 10 · For the grown-up Five Little Ducks · Sunday, January 10
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 7 months. Prop him with a cushion on the far side of the hill, facing the basket, so every duck rises over the top and drops out of sight. Gone and back is the funniest thing available to him this month. On the duck line he babbles back at the quacking, so leave him a gap between verses.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

Wrap him well for the pond. At 7 months a bank full of birds moving against gray water is the biggest thing he has been shown all week. Keep him off the ground at the edge. Twenty minutes in that cold is plenty.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Why she wants the same rhyme forty times.

The fortieth Five Little Ducks is not the same event for her that it is for you. The first few passes take everything she has to follow the tune. Once the tune runs on its own, she has room to hear the words. Once the words are free, she notices the number dropping by one every verse, and after that she finds the joke in the last line. Repetition buys her the spare capacity to attend to the next layer down. Research on toddler word learning keeps landing in the same place: a few books read over and over beat a wide rotation for what stays. Sing it again.

⚠️

Safety: The clothespins and the small rhyme-bag objects are choke-sized, so they come off the floor before Kreston does. Puddle ice this month is thin, so keep her off the frozen edge of anything deeper than her boot. If you take the pond option this afternoon, hold her hand at the water, scatter the food from well back, and stay between both children and the bank.

The Spoon and the Saucepan

You need: 1 saucepan · 1 wooden spoon · everybody's name.

  1. Turn the pan upside down on the floor between you and give her the spoon.
  2. Say her name in pieces and hit the pan once for each piece. AZ-LYN, two hits. KRES-TON, two. BROOK-LYN, two.
  3. Let her do yours, then let her do words that are not names. Hit whatever she says, however many pieces she reckons it has.

The Kitchen Drum Kit

⏱️ 60 min🧰 8 items

You need: 1 large cookie tin or a large empty can, 1 plastic tub with a lid, 1 cereal box, 1 saucepan, Packing tape, 2 wooden spoons, 1 dish towel, to mute one drum, 1 permanent marker

  1. Line the tin, the tub, the cereal box and the saucepan along the floor and tape their bases down so they stop traveling.
  2. Hit each one and let her say which is high and which is low. Stuff the dish towel into the box, hit it again, and she hears the same drum go dull.
  3. Names first, one hit per piece. Everyone in the house, then the neighbors, then the cat, then people she has invented.
  4. Move on to food for longer words. BREAD is one hit. BA-NA-NA is three. SPA-GHET-TI is four and she will want that one over and over.
  5. Play a rhyme line by line. TWIN-KLE TWIN-KLE LIT-TLE STAR, one hit per piece. Number the drums one to four in marker if she starts calling for a particular one.
  6. She plays something short and you copy it back, then you play and she copies. Keep them to three hits.

💡Say the word out loud while you hit it, every time. She is matching her mouth to her hand.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

Stamping Out the Names

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Walk the street and stamp what you pass. GATE is one stamp. LAMP-POST is two. FIRE HY-DRANT is three. Frozen puddles sit in the shade all day this month and a stamp on thin ice gives her a crack and a splinter pattern. She names the thing, she stamps it, and you take her count.

The Pattern You Can Hear

She lays a row of objects along the floor, gives each one a sound, and plays the row left to right.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: 8 spoons, 8 plastic or paper cups, 8 socks, 1 long strip of paper, or a line of masking tape on the floor, 1 marker, The drum kit from this morning

  1. Run the masking tape in a long line down the floor, or lay the paper strip out. That is the row.
  2. Start it off yourself. Spoon, cup, spoon, cup, spoon, cup, saying each one aloud. Ask her what comes next and wait through the silence.
  3. Give every object a sound. Spoon is a tap on the tin, cup is a slap on the tub, sock is silence. She will fill the row with socks.
  4. Play the row left to right, pointing at each object as its sound comes. Then again, faster. Then again with her pointing and you playing.
  5. Hand the row over. She builds the next one and you play it back, note for note, including the row that is seven socks and a spoon.
  6. Take one object out of the middle of a repeating row and play it again. Ask her what went missing.
  7. Photograph the last row before you clear it up, then let her play it from the photo.

💡Leave her patterns alone. A row that breaks its own rule is a row she made a decision about.

Day 11 · For the grown-up The Beat in Every Word · Monday, January 11
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 7 months and his babble has gone into long strings, ba-ba-ba-ba, each with a beat in it. Sit him well back from the kit with a plastic tub turned over and let him slap it flat handed. Answer him in his own rhythm: he gives you four, you give four back. He will wait for your turn.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He goes on the row. Put him at one end with a cushion behind him and let his sock be the last object in the pattern. At 7 months he reaches across his own middle, so set a spoon past his opposite shoulder and watch him twist over for it. Every time you play the row, end on him.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Rhythm and reading are more connected than they look.

Clapping BA-NA-NA into three pieces is reading practice, three years before she meets a letter. Reading asks her to hear that a word breaks into parts, hold those parts in order, and match them onto shapes on a page. The hearing comes first and beat is how children get at it. Preschoolers who can keep time with a steady pulse score higher on the sound-awareness tests that predict later reading, and the link survives once you account for age and vocabulary. Every rhyme sung in this house since Friday has run that machinery. The drums make it loud enough for her to catch herself doing it.

⚠️

Safety: A saucepan banged at close range is loud enough to hurt a 7-month-old's ears. Keep Kreston an arm's length back from the kit, give him his own quiet tub, and stop the session before it turns into hitting for volume. Wooden spoons swing at exactly his head height.

Finding the Darkest Corner

You need: 1 flashlight · every door in the house · her.

  1. Walk her round with the flashlight off, shutting doors and pulling curtains as you go. Stand in each room for a slow count of ten and let your eyes adjust.
  2. Ask her which one is darkest. Bathrooms and the cupboard under the stairs tend to win.
  3. Test the winner. Shine the flashlight at the ceiling and watch the circle arrive. Leave those curtains shut for the rest of the day.
Materials, laid out d12-materials.png

Day 12 · The main event Twinkle, Twinkle · Tuesday, January 12

🎨 MAKE
The main event · 9:15–10:15 AM

The Star Cup

⏱️ 60 min🧰 7 items

You need: 3–4 paper cups, or squares of dark card, 1 flashlight with fresh batteries, 1 metal skewer, or a sharpened pencil (adult only), 1 marker, Masking tape, 1 old magazine to push down onto, A room that goes dark with the door shut

  1. Sit her at the table with a cup and the marker and let her dot a pattern over the base and the sides. Ten or fifteen dots is plenty. A hundred dots makes a lamp.
  2. Stand the cup on the old magazine and push the skewer through each dot. You do all the pushing, she counts them off as they go.
  3. Make a second cup with a different pattern and let her name them both.
  4. Take the cups and the flashlight into the dark room. Flashlight pointing up, cup over the end of it, a strip of tape round the join if the fit is loose.
  5. Light off. Her stars land on the ceiling and travel when you tilt the flashlight. Lie on your backs underneath and sing the rhyme.
  6. Hand her the flashlight. It will go across the wall, the floor and your face.

💡Give the stars some distance. A cup held close to the ceiling throws a tight patch. Down at floor level the same cup throws a sky.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

The Sleeping Street

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Walk the usual route hunting for things that have shut down for winter. Buds on the bare twigs are sealed tight and will sit there until March. Ask her where the birds go at night, take her answer at face value, then go and look at the places she might be right about. The light goes not long after five this month.

Outdoors d12-outside.png

Kreston's Own Song

Twinkle, Twinkle carries a tune the whole house already owns, so the words can be about anything. Azlyn picks what goes in the verse, and she picks her brother.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 4 items

You need: The star cup and flashlight, Your phone, to record, Paper and crayons for the picture that goes with the song, Kreston's blanket

  1. Ask Azlyn what Kreston did today. Write it down as she says it, including the parts that did not happen.
  2. Pick four items off the list. The daft ones survive, and she does the choosing.
  3. Fit them to the tune a line at a time, singing each line the moment you have it so she hears whether it lands. Too many pieces crammed into a line is the usual trouble.
  4. Sing the finished verse twice so she has it in her. Then let her change a word.
  5. Record it on your phone, her singing and you underneath her. One take. Do not ask her for a tidier version.
  6. She draws the picture while the recording plays back. Kreston's blanket goes over her lap, or over him.
  7. Play it to Kreston sat on your knee facing his sister. He will hunt for where the sound comes from and find her face at the end of it.

💡Put the recording somewhere you will find it again. A three-year-old singing a song she made up about her brother disappears into a phone.

  • Draw the picture and skip the recording.
  • Star cup and flashlight on the ceiling for an hour, nothing else.
  • Sing the old words in four voices and let her pick a winner.
🌳 Out again · pick one
  • Swimming, and she can sing in the changing room
  • Indoor playground if the pool is shut or the line is out the door
  • The library, a day early
  • A warm cafe and a window, if nobody has the energy for a pool
  • Home, with the star cup and the curtains shut
Day 12 · For the grown-up Twinkle, Twinkle · Tuesday, January 12
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 7 months. Lay him on his back in the dark room for five minutes with the star cup on. He follows a slow-moving light across a whole ceiling now, and he will reach across his own body after one that crosses over him. Keep the beam off his face.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He swims too. At 7 months he sits supported in the water and reaches for anything floating within a hand's reach, so take an upturned cup in and let him chase it. Your hands stay on him the whole time he is in the water. Sing the star song at him in there, where the tiled echo turns your voice into something new. Twenty minutes, then out before he cools.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Why a wind-down object works better than a wind-down instruction.

Telling a lit-up three-year-old to calm down hands her the entire job. She has to notice the state, want it changed, and run the change herself, and she can manage about one of those on a good evening. An object takes the work off her. The star cup comes out, the big light goes off, the same song plays, and the sequence does the slowing for her. She has met that order often enough that the first step predicts the rest, so her body starts settling at the cup rather than at the bed. You already run this with the bath and the books. The cup joins the end of the line tonight.

⚠️

Safety: The skewer is adult-only and goes back in the drawer between cups, not on the table. If the flashlight takes button cells, tape the compartment shut; a swallowed button battery burns through a child's throat within hours. At the pool, Kreston stays in arm's reach in the water, every second.

Lining Up the Bears

You need: 10 soft toys · 1 blanket · a stretch of floor.

  1. Tip out the basket of ten soft toys you gathered last night and let her line all ten along the edge of the blanket, in whatever order she wants.
  2. Count the row together, touching each one as the number comes out. Let her tell you their names and write them down.
  3. Ask her who is going over the edge first. Whoever she picks goes on the end until 9:15.

Roll Over, Roll Over

⏱️ 60 min🧰 5 items

You need: 10 soft toys, 1 blanket, A bed, or a mattress or duvet on the floor, Paper and a marker for the countdown, 2 pillows as a barrier at the edge

  1. Put the mattress or the duvet on the floor, or use the bed with both pillows packed along the open side. Everybody goes over an edge this morning, so the edge wants to be low.
  2. Lay the ten toys along the blanket in the order she made, with her at one end of the row.
  3. Sing the verse. On "roll over" everyone rolls, toys included, and the one on the end goes off the side.
  4. Count who is left after every verse, touching each one, then write the new number on the paper. Nine. Eight. Seven.
  5. Let her say the number that opens the next verse. She will skip one, so count the row again and find out who is right.
  6. The last verse has one left and nobody to roll into. Sit in that, then let her throw all ten back on and start again.

💡The fallen toys land in a heap and she will want them back up. Keep the heap where she can see it growing.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

Counting the Doors to Number Ten

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Walk down one side of the street reading the house numbers out loud. Find number one and walk as far as number ten, and let her spot each numeral on the gate before you say it. Odd on one side and even on the other will bother her, and it is worth crossing the road to sort out.

The Bun Shop

Five Currant Buns in a Baker's Shop wants a shop, a baker and somebody with money in their hand.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: 1 cereal box, for five bun circles (or five real bread rolls if you have them), Scissors (adult only), Crayons for the currants, 1 tray, 1 shoebox as the register, 10 card coins, cut from the same box

  1. Cut five circles from the cereal box and ten coins from what is left. She draws the currants on, as many per bun as she likes.
  2. Set the tray on a low table as the counter and the shoebox behind it as the register. She is the baker, and the shop opens when she says.
  3. Count the buns onto the tray out loud. Five, touching each one.
  4. Sing the verse, walk up with a coin, buy one bun and carry it away. She hands the bun over and puts the coin in the register herself.
  5. After each sale, ask how many are left and let her count the tray from the start. Wait out the recount.
  6. Sell all five, then swap. She counts the coins out of the register one at a time into your hand.
  7. Shut the shop. Count the five coins in your hand and the five buns beside them, and stack both on the tray.

💡Do the buying in real time. A pause between sales, a walk to the door, a knock before you come in. She has to hold the number while the shop waits.

  • Real rolls, and eat the stock at snack time.
  • Set the shop up and let her sell to the ten bears instead.
  • Draw a shop front on a flattened box and stop there.
🌳 Out again · pick one
  • Indoor playground, and the quiet hour before school pickup if there is one
  • The library, if indoor playground is packed
  • The park in the cold, for twenty minutes and hot chocolate after
  • A friend's house, with the rhyme bag in your coat pocket
  • The indoor play center, if the weather has shut everything else down
Day 13 · For the grown-up Ten in the Bed · Wednesday, January 13
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 7 months. Sit him at the foot of the mattress with a cushion behind him and hand him each toy as it comes off the edge. He takes it, turns it over, moves it to his other hand, then drops it. Keep him off the rolling surface.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

Indoor playground at 7 months means the baby corner and nothing beyond it. He sits without help now, so put him on the mats with two soft blocks in reach and let the older children run past him. Half an hour, before the noise catches up with him.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Counting words come long before counting means anything.

Azlyn can chant to ten and still not know that the last word she said is the answer. Rote counting arrives first, as a song with numbers in it. The idea underneath, that the number you land on tells you how many there are, takes another year or so and it arrives through touching. One finger on one bear as one word leaves her mouth is the whole bridge, and so is a bun going off the tray and the tray having one fewer on it. Both were in today. Ask her how many and let her recount from one every single time, because starting again from one is the work at three.

⚠️

Safety: Ten in the Bed ends with somebody going over the edge. Do it on a mattress on the floor, or pillow the drop side and stay on it. Card coins only; real coins are the classic swallowed object at this age, and Kreston will be under the table hunting for whatever rolled.

Handing Out the Instruments

You need: the week's shakers, drums and spoons in one basket · a hat each.

  1. Put the basket down in the middle of the floor and let her hand the instruments out. She decides who gets what, including what you get.
  2. Hats on. Anything counts: a sun hat, a woolly one, a saucepan.
  3. Everyone plays their own thing at once for thirty seconds, then stops dead the moment she says stop. Do that twice and leave it until 9:15.

Up the Hill and Down Again

⏱️ 60 min🧰 5 items

You need: 4–6 sofa cushions, The week's shakers, drums and spoons, 1 sheet of paper, 1 wooden spoon and tape, for a flag, A hat each, 1 taped shaker for Kreston

  1. Build the hill. Four to six cushions stacked in the middle of the floor, wide enough to walk up and firm enough to stand on at the top.
  2. Tape the sheet of paper to the wooden spoon for a flag. She decides what goes on the flag and she carries it.
  3. Line up behind the flag with the instruments and the hats. March round the room once to get the step going, everyone starting on the same foot.
  4. Sing the Grand Old Duke of York. Up the cushions on "up", down the other side on "down".
  5. Halfway up and halfway down, stop dead on the word and hold it. Hold it longer than feels comfortable. She will ask for it eight times.
  6. Tape Kreston's shaker twice round and check the seal, then bring him into the line for the last two runs.

💡March slower than feels right. Ten thousand men come down that hill at half the speed you would walk it.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

In Step Round the Block

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

March the block. Left, right, left, right, called out loud, everyone setting off on the same foot. She loses the step inside twenty paces and finds it again. Halt at each corner and freeze for a count of five. January sidewalks are wet or salted, so drop the calling for a stretch and listen to the boots instead.

The Whole House Parade

The parade needs a route, and she draws it before anybody marches anywhere.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: 1 large sheet of paper for the route map, 1 marker, Masking tape to mark the stops on the floor, The instruments and the flag, A hat each, Your phone, to record the last run

  1. Spread the big sheet on the floor and draw the downstairs as one long line. Front door, hall, kitchen, living room, back to the door. She adds the rooms you forget.
  2. Mark four or five stops along the line, one per doorway. She picks a rhyme for each stop and you draw a small picture of it on the map.
  3. Tape an X on the floor at each stop so the band knows where to halt.
  4. Run it once with you leading. Play and march between the stops, halt on the X, everyone sings that doorway's rhyme.
  5. Run it again with Azlyn out front and the flag in her hand. She sets the speed, and the speed will be wrong.
  6. Third run, Kreston leads from your hip and Azlyn walks behind him with the drum.
  7. Record the last run on your phone, walking backwards in front of the band. Sit on the floor together and watch it once.

💡Let the route be daft. A parade that goes through the bathroom and out again is a better parade than a sensible one.

Day 14 · For the grown-up The Marching Band · Thursday, January 14
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 7 months and rides this one in the carrier, where the bounce of your step goes straight through him. Babies pick a beat up through the body long before they pick it out by ear. Sing the same four lines the whole way round.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

Take him into the hardware store in the carrier facing out. At 7 months the high shelves, the fluorescent lights and the racket of a big store are work for him, so twenty minutes is enough. Back home he gets his taped shaker for the last parade run, checked once more before it reaches his hands.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Why moving together matters more than moving.

Marching in step with Azlyn does something that dancing on your own round the kitchen does not. Move in time with another person and you both come away more inclined to help each other, and it shows up young. Bounce a fourteen-month-old in time with you and he hands back an object you drop more often than a baby bounced out of time. Four-year-olds show something like it after they have made music together. Shared rhythm reads as belonging, at any age, which is most of what a nursery rhyme has ever been for. Everything sung in this house since Friday has been two or four people locking onto one beat. Today it has hats.

⚠️

Safety: Build the hill low and wide, and stay within arm's reach the whole time she is standing on the top. A stack of cushions slides apart under a three-year-old's feet. Tape Kreston's shaker all the way round twice and check the seal every time before it reaches his hands. In the marching line, keep the spoons and shakers clear of his head; in the carrier it sits at swinging height.

January · Week 3

Kindness & Community 💛

January 15 – January 21, 2027 · Days 15–21

Most of the kindness around Azlyn happens out of her sight. The shopping arrives, the heating comes on, somebody made the dinner. This week she does it herself seven times over: a verse for every person in the house, a show for an audience of one, bird cakes for a frozen January, three real jobs before lunch, soup for the neighbors, a box of her own toys given away, cookies and cards on Thursday. One thread runs under all of it. The Good Thing Jar goes on the kitchen table on Friday and takes a paper strip every time somebody here does something for somebody else, and nobody reads a single strip until Day 21.

Martin Luther King Jr. Day lands on Monday, and Day 18 marks it with work. She gets three jobs she can finish before lunch and a pot of soup after it, and half of that pot leaves the house before dinner. Azlyn chooses which house it goes to and carries the jar to the door herself.

🧒 What Azlyn will learn
  • Making up a verse to a tune she knows. Holding the beat, feeling where the line has to land, and getting words there before the bar runs out.
  • Running a show start to finish. Waiting behind a curtain, coming out on her name, doing three items in the order she chose, and ending it.
  • Real jobs with a real result. Six potatoes scrubbed go in the soup, socks come back as pairs, soft vegetables get cut with a table knife she controls.
  • Choosing what to give and handing it over. A toy box into a stranger's hands, a jar of soup next door, cookies on three doorsteps.
  • Plain words for how people look. Skin, hair and eyes named out loud, and a crayon found for her own arm, yours and Kreston's.
👶 KRESTON THIS WEEK

Kreston is 7 months this week. He reaches across his own body for something sitting on his far side, moves it from hand to hand, and babbles in long strings that run like sentences.

The Big Book of Little Days · JanuaryWeek 3 · opener →
🌍 Around the world Week 3 · read it on Day 15

Southern Africa & Ubuntu 💛

The Nguni languages of southern Africa carry a word for the idea that a person is made a person by other people: ubuntu. The full saying, umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu, comes out in English as "a person is a person through other people." Desmond Tutu spent years explaining it to audiences who wanted a one-word translation, and no single English word holds it.

✨
Try it

Cook one pot tonight and stand it in the middle of the table. Everyone serves themselves from the same dish, Azlyn included, and she passes the spoon on.

The Big Book of Little Days · JanuaryWeek 3 · around the world →
Around the world w3-world.png
👩 What you'll learn
  • Verses she invents are worth more than verses she repeats
  • Performing for one person is enough
  • Kindness has to be visible before it can be learned
  • The age where they want to help is right now, and it's brief
  • Giving feels good only when the child does the giving
  • Children notice difference early, and silence teaches something
  • Gratitude is a skill, and it starts with noticing
Did you know

In Zulu, hello is sawubona, and it means "I see you."

Week 3: Kindness & Community 💛

Opening activity · 8:00–9:00 AM

Who the Song Is For

You need: paper, 4–5 sheets · 1 pen · the kitchen table.

  1. Ask her to name everyone who lives in this house. Write one name at the top of each sheet in big letters and let her choose which comes first.
  2. Pick the tune. Twinkle Twinkle, Frère Jacques, Happy Birthday, anything she sings unprompted. Sing it once with the words it came with.
  3. Ask her one true thing about the first person. Write the answer under the name. That line opens the song at 9:15.
