Day 15 · The main event The Made-Up Song · Friday, January 15
⏱️ 9:15 onward
🎨 MAKE
The main event · 9:15–10:15 AM

A Verse for Each Person

⏱️ 60 min🧰 5 items

You need: Paper, 4–5 sheets, one per person, 1 pen, 1 wooden spoon as a microphone, 1 saucepan and a second wooden spoon as a drum, Your phone, to record one take

  1. Sing the tune you chose this morning once with her name in it, so she hears the shape before she has to make one.
  2. Hand her the spoon and take the first sheet. Say the name at the top and let her sing. Write it down word for word, wrong grammar included.
  3. Keep a slow beat on the upturned saucepan underneath her. The beat carries her over the gap where the words run out.
  4. Work through every sheet. Do not offer her a rhyme and do not tidy a line she has sung. Kreston's verse will be about his feet.
  5. Read the whole thing back as one song and put her own name in the last line.
  6. Record one take on your phone. One. Sing it again afterwards with your hands free.

💡She will change the words on the second singing and be certain the new ones were always there. Write those underneath instead of correcting her. Both versions are hers.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

The Singing Walk

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Take the song out and sing it down the street. Cold January air carries a voice further than she expects, and she will hear her own noise come back off the houses. Sing your verse first so she sees a grown adult do it outdoors. Let her pick who gets a verse: a dog, a parked van, the woman at the bus stop.

🎨 MAKE
Second main event · 1:00–2:30 PM

The Good Thing Jar

The jar lands on the kitchen table today and stays all week. Good things go in on paper strips, and on Thursday you tip the lot out and read them.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: 1 clean jar with a lid, or a plastic tub, Paper cut into 20–30 strips, 1 pen, Crayons, Masking tape, Stickers if you have them

  1. Give her the empty jar and the crayons and leave her to decorate it. Tape covers a lot. So do stickers.
  2. Write THE GOOD THING JAR on a strip of tape and let her stick it on crooked.
  3. Cut the paper into strips together. Twenty is plenty and thirty is better.
  4. Walk the house room by room. In each room, name one thing somebody did for somebody else today: the tea you made, the toy Azlyn handed Kreston, the door Joseph shut.
  5. Write each one on a strip, read it out loud, and hand it to her to post. She posts every strip.
  6. Do three strips about her without using the word good or the word girl. Name the action: Azlyn carried the basket to the door.
  7. Put the jar where she can reach it. Anybody can post one, any time, and nobody reads them until Thursday.

💡Write what the person did, never what the person is. "Azlyn shared the cookie" is something she can do again tomorrow. "Azlyn is kind" is a verdict, and a verdict is harder to live with.

The Big Book of Little Days · January · Week 3Day 15 · afternoon →
Finished result d15-result.png
✨ Afternoon alternatives
  • Decorate the jar, post one strip, and leave the week to fill it.
  • Draw the good things instead of writing them, one per strip.
  • Post strips for people outside the house: grandparents, the woman at the store.
  • Tape a paper chain to the wall and add a link for each one.
🌳 Out again · pick one
  • Playgroup, and the song goes with her if she wants an audience
  • A friend's house, one child, one hour
  • The park, for whoever needs the noise taken out of them
  • A café with a window seat and one hot drink you get to finish
  • The corner store, and she carries the basket to the register
Day 15 · For the grown-up The Made-Up Song · Friday, January 15
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 7 months and babbling in long strings now, which is singing with the words still missing. Sit him on the floor with a wooden spoon of his own and the upturned plastic tub while Azlyn works. He bangs it, and the noise lands in the middle of her song instead of beside it. Set the spoon down on his far side once or twice, because reaching across his own body is new this month and worth the stretch.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

Cut him two or three strips from thicker paper and let him crumple them while Azlyn posts hers. At 7 months he moves a thing from one hand to the other and back, and paper that crackles holds him longer than a toy that stays silent. Keep his strips too big for his mouth.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Verses she invents are worth more than verses she repeats.

Azlyn can sing back a nursery rhyme she has heard two hundred times, and that is memory doing its work. Making up a verse asks for something harder. She has to hold the tune, feel where the beats fall, and land a line that fits before the bar runs out. Adults pay for lessons in that. She does it at three because nobody has told her it is difficult. Writing the lines down changes the transaction, because the words she pulled out of nothing now exist on paper and get read back to her. Children who invent language rather than recite it build a stronger sense of what words can do.

⚠️

Safety: A glass jar carried by a three-year-old with Kreston on the floor is a bad combination. Use a plastic tub, or keep the jar on the table and let her post the strips standing up. Loose paper goes in his mouth, so sweep before you put him down.

Opening activity · 8:00–9:00 AM

The One Ticket

You need: card or a cereal box · crayons · scissors (yours) · 1 pen.

  1. Tell her a show is happening at 1:00 and one ticket exists. She decides who gets it.
  2. Cut a rectangle of card and hand it over. The picture on the front is whatever the show will be about, so she chooses that too.
  3. Write ADMIT ONE along the bottom and let her copy the shapes underneath. It stands against the kettle until she walks it round at 10:30.

⏱️ 9:15 onward

The main event · 9:15–10:15 AM

The Kitchen Stage

⏱️ 60 min🧰 7 items

You need: 1 sheet or thin blanket for the curtain, 2 dining chairs, 6 clothespins or binder clips, 1 flashlight as a spotlight, 1 cushion for the audience seat, The ticket she made at 8:00, Card and crayons for a sign

  1. Stand a chair either side of the doorway, backs facing into the room, and clip the sheet across both backs so it hangs as a curtain she can drag aside. You hang it, she tells you it is crooked.
  2. Put the cushion on the floor a few paces back. The auditorium seats one.
  3. Ask her what the show is. Take the first three answers and write them on the card in order: a song, a dance, a jump off the bottom stair.
  4. Rehearse the opening on its own. She waits behind the sheet, you say her name, she pulls the curtain and comes out. Do it four times. The coming out is the part she is learning.
  5. Run all three items once in order with the flashlight on her from the cushion.
  6. Stop while she still wants more. The show is at 1:00.

💡Resist adding a fourth item. Three things she can hold in her head beat six she has to be reminded of, and a show she runs unprompted is one she owns.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

Posting the Invitation

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Take the ticket off the kettle and walk it to whoever is coming at 1:00. If the audience lives in this house, she posts it through your own front door and you act surprised when it lands on the mat. A grandparent up the road means the whole walk, with the mail slot flap hers to push. Gloves on. January makes that flap colder than she expects.

Outdoors d16-outside.png

🎨 MAKE
Second main event · 1:00–2:30 PM

The One-Person Show

At one o'clock the ticket holder sits down, and everybody else in the house is either backstage or out of the room.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 7 items

You need: The stage and curtain, The ticket, 1 flashlight, 1 hairbrush as a microphone, 1 saucepan drum, 2 cookies and a drink for the audience, Your phone, to film one song

  1. Seat the audience. One cushion, one person, cookies and a drink in their hands. Nobody watches from the doorway.
  2. Take the delivered ticket at the door and tear the corner off. She will care about this more than any other thirty seconds of the afternoon.
  3. Announce her by her full name from behind the curtain, then get out of the way. Flashlight on, big light off.
  4. Watch the whole thing. No correcting the running order, no feeding her the words. Clap after each item.
  5. Ask for one of them again. An encore from an audience of one is the point of the afternoon.
  6. Swap over. She takes the cushion and the second cookie, you go behind the curtain and do a song.
  7. Leave the stage up. She runs the show again at 4:15 with nobody watching, and that version belongs to her.

💡Film one song at the start, then put the phone face down. She can tell a parent watching from a parent recording, and she plays to the room she is given.

The Big Book of Little Days · January · Week 3Day 16 · afternoon →
Finished result d16-result.png
✨ Afternoon alternatives
  • One song from behind the sofa. Same idea, four minutes.
  • A puppet show over a chair back with two socks.
  • She directs and you perform the whole thing.
  • Call a grandparent and do the show over the phone.
🌳 Out again · pick one
  • The farm, for the indoor barn and whatever gets fed at three
  • Indoor playground, if the farm has turned to mud
  • The park, and the show gets performed again on the climbing frame
  • A friend's house, and a second audience of one
  • The pet store, twenty minutes, nothing bought
Day 16 · For the grown-up The Show for One · Saturday, January 16
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 7 months, and a curtain that opens and shuts is the best offer he has had all week. Sit him at the audience end and let Azlyn drag the sheet across and back. He holds onto the idea of a thing after it leaves his sight, and every pull tests that. Keep the sheet clear of his face.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He goes to the farm in the carrier, where at 7 months the smell of a barn is new information and he goes quiet in it because he is working. Keep him clear of anything with teeth and wash both pairs of hands before anybody eats. Back home he gets the hairbrush microphone, and the shouting into it is aimed at a person now.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Performing for one person is enough.

A three-year-old singing to a room of adults is doing a different job from a three-year-old singing to one. The audience of one keeps her attention on the thing itself, on the song and the order and the ending she planned, with no crowd to read. She gets the whole arc: waiting behind a curtain, starting, finishing, watched the entire way through. Children build social confidence in doses about this size. One person who stays until the end teaches her that a thing has a finish, and that finishing it is the good part. Two people watching is not twice as good to her. It is twice as much to keep track of.

⚠️

Safety: She will climb on a dining chair to reach the curtain. You hang it, she stands back. Nothing tied at neck height, no cord left running across the doorway, and no draped sheet anywhere over Kreston. Take the curtain down before bed.

Opening activity · 8:00–9:00 AM

The Window Count

You need: the window with the best view · paper · 1 crayon · two chairs.

  1. Pull the chairs up to the glass and sit with her before the house is awake.
  2. Every bird that lands in view gets a mark on the paper. She makes the mark, you keep still. Count them out loud at the end.
  3. Ask her where a bird finds food in January with the ground frozen. Do not answer. You are making some at 9:15.
Materials, laid out d17-materials.png
The Big Book of Little Days · January · Week 3Day 17 · morning →
Day 17 · The main event Feeding the Birds · Sunday, January 17
⏱️ 9:15 onward
🎨 MAKE
The main event · 9:15–10:15 AM

The Bird Cakes

⏱️ 60 min🧰 6 items

You need: 250 g lard or solid vegetable fat, left out to soften (smooth peanut butter works instead), 500 g birdseed, or rolled oats, breadcrumbs, raisins and sunflower seeds mixed, 4–6 clean yogurt pots or empty cans, String, 3 feet, 1 large mixing bowl and 1 wooden spoon, 1 skewer or the point of the scissors, adult only, for the string hole

  1. Make a hole in the base of each pot with the skewer, thread a loop of string through and knot it inside. Yours to do, and she counts the pots.
  2. Tip the softened fat into the bowl and let her get both hands in it. It takes her a minute to commit.
  3. Add the seed, oats, crumbs and raisins a scoop at a time and let her squeeze until the mix holds in a lump. One part fat to two parts dry, by eye.
  4. Pack the mix into the pots and let her press it down with her fists, string held out of the way.
  5. Into the fridge to set. They come out at 1:00.
  6. Wash both pairs of hands with soap before you touch the counter.

💡Let her overfill one pot and underfill another. Birds have no standards, and the two she got wrong are the two she watches hardest.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

Where the Birds Are

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Walk the usual route with one job: find where the birds already are. In January they cluster in thick hedges, in anything with berries still on it, and in the tangle at the back of a yard. Stand still under a hedge for a minute and listen before either of you looks up. Let her choose the branch the cakes hang from on the way home.

Outdoors d17-outside.png
The Big Book of Little Days · January · Week 3Day 17 · main event →
Day 17 · Afternoon Feeding the Birds · Sunday, January 17
⏱️ 1:00 onward
🎨 MAKE
Second main event · 1:00–2:30 PM

The Feeding Station

The cakes come out of the fridge set hard, and the afternoon happens at the window under a blanket.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 7 items

You need: The set bird cakes, String and scissors, 1 shallow dish, an old plant saucer or a takeout lid, A pitcher of warm water to thaw the dish, 1 chair pulled to the window, Paper and 1 crayon for the tally, 1 blanket

  1. Run warm water round the outside of each pot and the cake slides out whole. Leave a long loop of string.
  2. Hang them where she can see them from the chair: low branches, the clothesline, a nail in the fence. She picks the spots, you tie the knots.
  3. Stand the shallow dish in the open, clear of any bush a cat could sit under, and pour the warm water in. Unfrozen water in January is harder to find than food.
  4. Scatter crumbs on the ground for the birds that will not use a feeder.
  5. Come in, pull the chair to the window and get under the blanket. The wait outlasts her patience on day one.
  6. Every arrival gets a mark on the tally, same as 8:00. Put the two sheets side by side at the end.
  7. Leave the tally and the crayon on the windowsill. She keeps marking it all week with nobody asking.

💡Twenty minutes of nothing is the normal result. Name the birds you both know, then let the quiet come back. A hide with a commentary running in it stops being a hide.

The Big Book of Little Days · January · Week 3Day 17 · afternoon →

✨ Afternoon alternatives
  • Hang one cake and put the water dish out.
  • Thread cereal hoops onto string and hang those instead.
  • Draw the birds she saw this morning from memory.
  • Press crumbs into an apple core and spike it on a twig.
🌳 Out again · pick one
  • The scooter or the balance bike, helmet on, to the end of the road and back
  • The park, counting birds there and back
  • A long loop with the stroller and no destination
  • Feed the ducks with the crusts she has been saving
  • The pet store and its seed aisle, if it is too wet to be out
Day 17 · For the grown-up Feeding the Birds · Sunday, January 17
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 7 months. Hold him up to the glass before you go out, tap where a bird lands and wait. He follows a pointing finger on a good day and stares at the finger on a bad one. Outside, stop the stroller under the hedge and let him turn his head toward a sound with nothing attached to it.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He faces Azlyn in the stroller while she scoots, so turn the seat round. At 7 months he tracks a moving thing across his whole field of view, and a sister on wheels is the best one going. Back at the window he sits on your lap and slaps the glass, which is a fair contribution to the tally.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Kindness has to be visible before it can be learned.

Azlyn cannot see most of the kindness around her. The shopping arrives, the heating comes on, and none of it looks to her like a choice anybody made. Feeding birds in January puts one act of care in front of her start to finish. The need is real, the animal is cold, and she is the one with her hands in the fat. Children copy what they can watch being done more than what they are told about, and a dish of thawed water on a frozen morning is a kindness with all its working shown.

⚠️

Safety: Loose birdseed on the floor near a seven-month-old who mouths everything, so sweep before you put Kreston down. Wash both pairs of hands after handling seed, fat and feeders. Use smooth peanut butter only, never whole or chopped nuts, and check for a nut allergy before you start. Keep the bird dish shallow and stand it where you can see it from the window, and tip it out before you put Kreston down anywhere near it, because a baby drowns in less water than that.

Opening activity · 8:00–9:00 AM

The Job Board

You need: 1 sheet of paper · 1 pen · crayons · masking tape.

  1. Draw three boxes down a sheet of paper and let her fill each with a picture of the job: the potatoes, the socks, the windows.
  2. Tape it to the kitchen door at her height, not yours.
  3. Tell her all three are real, all three are hers, and nobody else is doing them today. She picks which goes first.
Materials, laid out d18-materials.png
The Big Book of Little Days · January · Week 3Day 18 · morning →
Day 18 · The main event The Helping Day · Monday, January 18
⏱️ 9:15 onward
🎨 MAKE
The main event · 9:15–10:15 AM

Three Real Jobs

⏱️ 60 min🧰 7 items

You need: 1 dishpan and warm water, 1 low stool, 6 potatoes and 1 small scrubbing brush, The sock basket, unsorted, 1 spray bottle of water, 2 cloths, 1 old towel for the floor

  1. The potatoes. Bowl of warm water on the towel, stool beside it, brush in her hand. Six scrubbed until the water goes brown, and she decides when one is finished.
  2. The socks. Tip the basket out and let her hunt for pairs. She will put a black one with a navy one, and those two go in the drawer as a pair.
  3. The windows. Spray bottle in one hand, cloth in the other, one low window or the back door glass. Smears are the finish.
  4. Hand each job over and move away from it. Ten minutes each is slow, and she has the whole hour.
  5. Say what she did rather than how it turned out. "The potatoes are washed and they go in the soup at 1:00" attaches the job to something.
  6. Do not redo any of it where she can see you. The window can wait.

💡Every job has to be one she can finish. A whole basket of socks is a wall. The same basket with the whites pulled out has an end on it.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

Taking the Trash Cans In

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Monday, and the trash cans are out. Wheel yours back down the path with her hands on the handle beside yours, then knock next door and bring theirs in too. She holds on and does almost none of the pulling, and she knows it. Walk the block after and let her pick up three pieces of litter with a bag over her hand.

Outdoors d18-outside.png
The Big Book of Little Days · January · Week 3Day 18 · main event →
Day 18 · Afternoon The Helping Day · Monday, January 18
⏱️ 1:00 onward
🎨 MAKE
Second main event · 1:00–2:30 PM

Soup for Two Houses

Today is Martin Luther King Jr. Day, marked by doing something for somebody else. Half of this pot leaves the house before dinner.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 8 items

You need: 1 onion, 3 carrots, the 6 potatoes she scrubbed this morning, 1 zucchini or a handful of mushrooms, soft for her knife, 1 can of chopped tomatoes or 2 bouillon cubes, 2 liters water, 1 table knife and 1 chopping board for her, 1 large pot and 1 ladle, 1 clean jar with a screw lid, 1 dish towel

  1. Set her up at the table with the board, the table knife and the soft vegetables. The hard ones are yours.
  2. Show her the grip once: fingers curled back, other hand flat on the blade, push down and forward. Then let her do it her own way.
  3. Everything she cuts goes in the pot, including the pieces the size of her fist. Soup forgives.
  4. Onto the stovetop with the tomatoes, the stock and the water. She stirs from the stool with your hand over hers, pan handle turned in.
  5. Thirty minutes of simmering, and in the gap she chooses which house gets the jar.
  6. Ladle half in once it has stopped steaming, screw the lid down, wrap the dish towel round it and hand it to her.
  7. Deliver it before dinner, or call ahead and take it tomorrow. She hands it over herself.

💡Do not give her a line to say at the door. Whatever comes out will be better than anything you could have written.

  • Sandwiches instead of soup, and half of them go next door.
  • She washes and you cook, and the whole pot stays here.
  • Bag up cans she chooses for the food bank.
  • Draw a card for the person getting the jar.
🌳 Out again · pick one
  • The woods loop, muddy in January and better for it
  • The riverside path, to see how high the water is
  • The neighborhood park, twenty minutes, then home to the pot
  • A drive to drop the jar off, with her holding it
  • The indoor play center, if the woods have washed out
Day 18 · For the grown-up The Helping Day · Monday, January 18
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 7 months and copies the shape of a job long before he can do one. Sit him on the towel with a dry cloth of his own and a wooden spoon, a full arm's length clear of the water. Raw potato breaks off in hard pieces under a gum, so the potatoes stay on her side. He bangs the spoon, hands it to you and waits for it back, which is the game of his month.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He goes in the carrier for the woods, facing out. At 7 months he grabs everything within reach, so keep low branches away from his hands and check what comes back in his fist. He stays out of the kitchen while the pot is on the stovetop, and gets the empty can and a wooden spoon once it is off.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

The age where they want to help is right now, and it's brief.

Azlyn wants the brush, the cloth and the spray bottle, because the work is real and she has watched you do it. Toddlers offer help without being asked from around eighteen months, and the offers thin out across the school years as the help keeps getting turned down for being slow. She scrubs six potatoes in the time you would take over twenty, and those six go in the pot in front of her. Take the offer while she is still making it, and let the standard be hers. The potatoes will come out with grit still on them. The offer is worth more this month than the potatoes are.

⚠️

Safety: The dishpan holds enough water to drown Kreston at 7 months, so he stays inside arm's reach of you the whole time it is down and it gets tipped out every time you step away from it. Hot pot on the stovetop with a three-year-old at counter height: pan handles turned in, she stirs from the stool with your hand on hers, and the soup goes into the jar cool enough to hold. The knives you use stay out of reach between cuts.

Opening activity · 8:00–9:00 AM

Keep or Give

You need: 8 of her own toys · a clear bit of floor · nothing else.

  1. Bring eight things she owns into the middle of the floor. You choose them, and pick ones she has not touched in a month.
  2. Two piles: keep and give. She decides every one and you say nothing.
  3. If all eight land in keep, that is the answer and you carry on. Tell her the box is going to a child who has none of this, and leave it there.

The Giving Box

⏱️ 60 min🧰 5 items

You need: 1 strong box or 2 sturdy bags, 1 damp cloth, Masking tape and 1 marker, 1 separate bag for anything broken, Paper and 1 pen for her list

  1. Start with clothes. Anything she has grown out of comes off the shelf, and she holds each thing once before it goes in.
  2. Move on to toys. She chooses. You get one veto for the whole morning, so hold onto it.
  3. She wipes every item with the damp cloth before it goes in. She is sending these out in good condition and her hands do that part.
  4. Anything broken goes in the separate bag. Broken things are trash, and she gets to be the one who says which is which.
  5. Ask her for one line about each toy, meant for the child who gets it. Write it word for word on a strip of tape and stick it on: THIS ONE ROLLS DOWN THE STAIRS.
  6. Tape the box shut, let her draw on the lid, and stand it by the front door where she walks past it.

💡She will pull one thing back out of the box. Let her, and say nothing about it. A child who is allowed to take one thing back puts three more in.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

Delivering the Box

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

The box goes today, while it still means something to her. Load it into the bottom of the stroller and walk it to the thrift store, the church porch or the family two streets over with a smaller child. Let her carry it the last twenty feet even though it is too big for her, and hand it across herself. Ask whoever takes it to tell her where it goes next.

Kreston's Posting Box

Something arrives in the house this afternoon instead of leaving it, and Azlyn makes it for her brother.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: 1 shoebox or empty wipes tub, Thick cardboard cut into discs the size of your palm, 8–10, 1 pair of scissors, adult only, Crayons and a marker, Masking tape, 1 scarf or wide ribbon to thread through and pull out

  1. Cut three or four hand-sized holes in the lid and one bigger one in the side. The scissors are yours throughout.
  2. Cut the cardboard into discs the size of your palm, eight to ten, counted out loud so she knows the number you started with.
  3. Hand her the crayons and the marker. Every disc gets decorated and so does the box. Write KRESTON on the lid in outline for her to fill in.
  4. Thread the scarf through the side hole so a hand's length hangs out, no more. He pulls, it keeps coming, and he comes back to it all afternoon.
  5. Show her how to post a disc through the lid, then hand the box over and let her teach him. You stay out of it.
  6. Sit behind them both and watch his hands. Posting is months beyond him, and the discs are still worth having.
  7. Count the discs back in at the end. The same number that went out.

💡Let her post the discs herself for the first ten minutes before he gets a look in. She spent the morning giving her own things away, and first go on his new toy is a fair trade.

  • Make him a ribbon pull from an old wipes tub instead.
  • Draw a picture for the child who gets the giving box.
  • Sort what is left on her shelf into rows and stop there.
🌳 Out again · pick one
  • Swimming, and she carries her own bag in
  • Indoor playground if the pool session is canceled
  • The library, a day early, for something to read in the bath
  • A warm café and a window, if the morning has used everybody up
  • The indoor play center
Day 19 · For the grown-up Giving It Away · Tuesday, January 19
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 7 months and everything in that box has been in his mouth at some point, so wipe as you pack. Give him one toy that is staying, a soft one of Azlyn's she has agreed to lend for the morning, and watch what happens when she takes it back. He does not mind yet. That window shuts somewhere around his first birthday.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He comes to the pool if he is coming. At 7 months he sits supported in the water and slaps at it with both hands, and he aims the splash at a person now. Twenty minutes, then out and dressed before he goes cold.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Giving feels good only when the child does the giving.

Sorting her toys while she is at playgroup and dropping the bag off yourself clears the cupboard. Azlyn takes nothing from it, because she was not in the room. The good feeling arrives through the doing: choosing it, holding it one last time, walking it to a door and putting it into a stranger's hands. Researchers who watch toddlers hand over treats find the pleasure shows up when the child does the handing, and less of it when the treat was never hers. She needs the whole sequence, including the part where it costs her something.

⚠️

Safety: Everything that goes in Kreston's box has to be bigger than his fist. No bottle caps, no coins, no small lids. Cut the discs palm-sized, count them in and out, and the scissors stay with you. The scarf comes out of the box the moment you stop watching. Swimming this afternoon. Both children stay within arm's reach in the water at all times, and no float or seat is a substitute for your hands.

Opening activity · 8:00–9:00 AM

Hands on the Table

You need: the kitchen table · her hands, yours and Kreston's · 1 hand mirror.

  1. Lay your hand flat on the table next to hers and ask what she notices. Take whatever answer arrives, including none.
  2. Bring Kreston's hand in and put all three side by side. Name the differences with nothing softened: bigger, smaller, darker, paler, more freckles.
  3. Hold the mirror so she sees her own face with yours beside it. Use the words skin, hair and eyes and let her use them back.

Finding the Right Crayon

⏱️ 60 min🧰 5 items

You need: Paper, 8–10 sheets, The whole crayon box, browns and pinks included, 1 hand mirror, Photos on your phone of the people she names, 1 pencil

  1. Tip the whole box out. Every color on the table, nothing sorted, nothing put back.
  2. She holds crayons against her own forearm one at a time until she finds the closest match. The hunting takes longer than you expect and it is the work.
  3. Do the same on your arm, then on Kreston's. Three people, three crayons, and she picks all three.
  4. Line the three up on the paper and let her see how close together they sit.
  5. Open the photos on your phone. She names people she knows and picks a crayon for each: grandparents, the girl from playgroup, the man at the store counter.
  6. She draws everybody in the colors she chose. Write the names on for her and put one on the fridge before lunch.

💡If she decides somebody's color is wrong, agree that skin comes in more colors than the box holds, and show her how to lay two crayons over each other.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

The Hello Walk

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Walk with one job: say hello to every person you pass and keep score of how many say it back. A Wednesday morning in mid-January hands you dog walkers and the mail carrier, so go where the people are: the row of stores, the bus stop, the school pickup line at eleven. She does the hello with you a step behind her, and she counts the answers on her fingers.

Three Phone Calls

Three people are expecting a call from Azlyn this afternoon. She calls each one and asks the same three questions.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: 1 phone, 3 people agreed and warned in advance, Paper and 1 pen, Crayons, This morning's drawings, 1 blanket and the sofa

  1. Choose the three questions together and write them big enough for her to see while she talks: What did you have for breakfast? What is the weather like? What made you laugh today?
  2. Get on the sofa under the blanket, phone on speaker, her drawings on her lap and the crayons within reach.
  3. Call the first one. She says hello, a long silence follows, and the person at the other end has been warned to wait through it. She asks the questions in her own order and forgets the third: prompt once, then leave it.
  4. Write each answer down as it comes and read the three back to her once you have hung up.
  5. She holds her drawing of that person up to the phone, which makes no sense and matters to her. Tell them what she drew, then she starts a fresh drawing of whoever is next while the number rings.
  6. Lay the three sheets side by side once the calls are done and find the one thing all three people said. There is always one.
  7. Turn each sheet over and let her draw what she was told: the weather at their window, the breakfast, the thing that made them laugh.

💡Three questions, thirty seconds each, and nobody asks her how preschool is going. A phone call with a job inside it is one she can do. If she is still going at two, she calls a fourth.

  • Record a voice message for each person instead of calling.
  • Mail the drawings to all three instead of calling.

  • The library, every two weeks, with her own book bag both ways
  • Indoor playground, if the library has a school group in
  • The store, and she chooses one thing off the list
  • The park on the way home, ten minutes, coats on
  • A café and the first new book read cover to cover
Day 20 · For the grown-up Same and Different · Wednesday, January 20
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 7 months and studies a face that does not look like the four he sees every day. Point him at people instead of the road. Babies his age hold a gaze longer on a new face, the first version of the noticing Azlyn is doing on paper. Back home, hold him in front of the mirror with Azlyn beside him.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He goes down in the library's picture-book corner. At 7 months he reads a board book by getting a corner into his mouth and turning it over. Hunt out books with real photographs of faces, hold one in front of him and see which face he stays with longest. Azlyn chooses his second one.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Children notice difference early, and silence teaches something.

Azlyn clocked skin color around her second birthday and has sorted people by it ever since, the same way she sorts crayons and socks. Saying nothing feels neutral from the inside. Children read an adult's silence as a signal that a subject is off limits, then fill the gap with an explanation of their own. Naming what she sees, in plain words with none of your anxiety in it, hands her the language before she invents worse for herself. The crayon she chose for her own arm and the one she chose for Kreston are different, and both drawings are on the fridge.

⚠️

Safety: The hand mirror is glass, so keep it in your hand or use a plastic one, and put it away when you finish. Crayons go off the floor while Kreston is down, because a snapped one is mouth-sized. The phone stays out of his reach between calls.

🌅 START
Opening activity · 8:00–9:00 AM

Reading the Jar

You need: the Good Thing Jar · the strips · the kitchen table.

  1. Tip the whole jar out and let her push the strips around with both hands. There should be twenty or more.
  2. Read every one out loud. All of them, including the four that say the same thing.
  3. Sort them into piles, one per person, and count each pile out loud. That count is how many cookies get cut at 9:15.

The main event · 9:15–10:15 AM

Thank-You Cookies

⏱️ 60 min🧰 9 items

You need: 200 g butter, softened, 100 g superfine sugar, 300 g all-purpose flour, plus extra for the board, 2 tbsp milk, 1 rolling pin, 1 cutter or an upturned glass, 1 baking tray and parchment paper, 1 cooling rack or a cold plate, Sprinkles, if you have them

  1. Butter and sugar in the bowl, flour on top. She rubs it through with her fingertips until the bowl looks like breadcrumbs. Both hands in, no spoon.
  2. Add the milk a spoon at a time and let her squeeze it into a dough. A dusting of flour fixes it if it sticks to her.
  3. Flour the board and roll it out to about a finger's thickness. Leave the thin patches where they are.
  4. She counts the shapes against the piles from 8:00 and keeps cutting until the numbers match. Re-roll the scraps twice, then the third lot is hers.
  5. Bake at 350°F for 12 to 15 minutes, until the edges turn gold. She stays at the table. You move the tray.
  6. Slide them onto the cold plate once they firm up, and count them again with her when they are cool.

💡Let her cut whatever shapes she wants. Somebody is getting a triangle with a thumbprint in it, and that person is getting the better cookie.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

The Cookie Round

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Bag the cookies in twos and walk them round. The neighbor who took the package in, the woman at the corner store, the friend who has had a rough month. She knocks, she hands them over, she says her own version of the words. Ten minutes a stop, so pick three doors and stop at three. Keep two back for the walk home.

The Thank-You Cards

Every strip in that jar has a name on it, and every one of those people gets a card this afternoon.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 7 items

You need: Card, or cereal boxes cut into rectangles, 8–10, Crayons and 1 glue stick, 1 pen for you, Stickers, The strips from the jar, Envelopes or folded paper, 1 stamp, if one is going in the mail

  1. Cut the card into rectangles and fold them. Cereal boxes work fine and the printed side goes on the inside.
  2. Take the strips one person at a time. Read them out loud, then ask her what the card should say.
  3. Write her words down word for word. THANK YOU FOR CARRYING ME UP THE STAIRS WHEN MY LEGS WERE TIRED. Do not shorten it or fix the grammar.
  4. She draws the thing they did on the front. The drawing will be unrecognizable and the person will recognize it, because her words sit underneath.
  5. She signs each one: a shape, a letter A, a single line, the same mark on every card so it becomes her signature.
  6. Stickers and glue on whatever needs them, then stack the finished cards next to the cookie bags by the door.
  7. One card goes in the mail with a stamp on it. Walk to the mailbox before dinner and let her drop it in.

💡Do the cards for the people in this house last, and find a reason to leave the room when she gets to yours.

Day 21 · For the grown-up Thank You Day · Thursday, January 21
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 7 months and the kitchen at 9:15 is hot, floury and no place for him. Set him up in the doorway with a wooden spoon and the saucepan, out of the kitchen and in your sight, and keep the flour bag off the floor because it goes straight in his mouth. On the round, wariness of an unfamiliar face is new this month, so keep him facing you when somebody leans in.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

Take him to the market in the carrier facing out and stop at one loud or bright stall. At 7 months he babbles in long runs and a busy street pulls it out of him, so answer him as though he said words. Give him a lidded can or an unopened box to hold while Azlyn hands the money over. Raw apple and raw carrot break off in hard pieces, so neither goes in his hands.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Gratitude is a skill, and it starts with noticing.

Prompting say thank you teaches Azlyn a word to produce on cue. The jar teaches the step underneath the word. All week she has watched for the things people did and heard them written down, so by Thursday she can name eleven of them. The noticing is the part that carries. A child who works out what somebody did for her, and then does something back, holds onto it longer than one reminded to be polite. She made a cookie for each name, and that is a thank you with a cost inside it. Her list will have the mail carrier on it and leave you off. Write it down the way she says it.

⚠️

Safety: The oven is on and the tray comes out at her eye level. She stays back from the door, the hot tray goes to the middle of the counter, and Kreston stays out of the kitchen while it moves. Raw dough is not a snack today.

Day 22
The Seven Pieces
The Big Book of Little Days · January · Week 3Day 21 · for the grown-up
January · Week 4

Puzzles & Problem Solving 🧩

January 22 – January 28, 2027 · Days 22–28

Seven days of problems that have real answers in them, and your job for most of the week is to sit on your hands. You cut a square into seven pieces and Azlyn tries to rebuild it, gets six different lids off, works out what has gone from a tray of eight things, sorts one pile twice under two different rules, and rolls a ball into three dead ends before she finds the way out. The pause before you help is the method. She solves more than you expect once nobody reaches in.

No holiday lands this week, so the thread running through it is cardboard. Friday's tangram, Saturday's jigsaw, Monday's pairs cards and Thursday's maze walls all come off the same flattened cereal boxes, and one day's offcuts are the next day's materials. Start the pile behind the sofa tonight. Tuesday is swimming, the fourth of the year, and Saturday's aquarium is the big outing.

🧒 What Azlyn will learn
  • Turning a shape until it fits. Tangram pieces go in flipped and backwards before they drop into the gap.
  • Six ways to open a thing. Screw, clip, zip, tape, knot and elastic band, each one asking her hands for something different.
  • Holding a set in her head. Eight objects on a tray, one taken away, and she names the gap.
  • Running two rules over one pile. A red spoon is a red thing at nine and a two-hands thing at ten.
  • Backing out of a dead end. She sees the route was wrong, goes back to the last corner and takes the other way.
👶 KRESTON THIS WEEK

Kreston is 7 months this week. He reaches across his own body for a toy, passes it from hand to hand, and babbles in long runs of bababa and dadada with the shape of sentences in them.

The Big Book of Little Days · JanuaryWeek 4 · opener →
🌍 Around the world Week 4 · read it on Day 22

China and the Tangram 🧩

The seven pieces on your table are Chinese and they are old. The puzzle is called qi qiao ban, seven boards of skill, and Chinese printers were selling books of tangram figures by the early 1800s. Sets traveled, and by 1818 Europe and America were in the middle of a tangram craze, thousands of shapes, every one using all seven pieces and nothing else.

✨
Try it

Cut her lunchtime sandwich into the same seven shapes and let her rebuild the square on the plate before she eats it.

The Big Book of Little Days · JanuaryWeek 4 · around the world →
Around the world w4-world.png
👩 What you'll learn
  • Sharing and turn-taking are different skills, and one is much easier
  • Being told what someone loves about you is different from being praised
  • Puzzles build a skill that has nothing to do with puzzles
  • Working memory is the thing she is building
  • Classification is quiet, invisible math
  • Describing before guessing is the whole skill
  • Dead ends are the point of a maze
Did you know

Two mathematicians proved in 1942 that only thirteen tangram shapes have no dents in the edges.

Cutting the Seven Pieces

You need: 1 of the cereal boxes you flattened last night · a ruler or any straight edge · 1 pencil · scissors (adult only).

  1. Cut an 8-inch square from the cereal box you flattened last night, then rule a line corner to corner and cut along it. Two big triangles. She holds the card flat while you cut.
  2. Cut one of those in half again, then work the other down into a medium triangle, two small ones, a square and a slanted four-sided piece.
  3. Seven pieces on the table and no picture yet. Let her push them round, then leave them until 9:15.

🎨 MAKE
The main event · 9:15–10:15 AM

Tangram Animals

⏱️ 60 min🧰 5 items

You need: The seven cut pieces, 4 sheets of paper for tracing outlines, 1 pencil and 1 permanent marker, 1 envelope or freezer bag to keep the set in, A clear table or a tray to work on

  1. Hand her all seven and ask her to make the square they came from. Leave her with it a while. She does not have to get it.
  2. Build a cat together on a sheet of paper: big triangle for the body, the square for the head, two small triangles for ears. She sets the ears.
  3. Draw round the finished cat in pencil, lift the pieces off and go over the outline in marker.
  4. Do a boat and a house the same way, tracing each one before you break it up.
  5. Let her invent the fourth. Trace it and write her name for it along the bottom, spelling and all.
  6. Everything goes in the envelope with TANGRAM on the front. She is back at it by 4:15.

💡When she pushes a piece in upside down, leave it. Turning a shape over until it drops into the gap is the skill, and your hand on the piece ends it.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

The Arrow Trail

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Walk out with a job: at every corner she lays an arrow of sticks, stones or scuffed gravel pointing the way you came. Four or five is plenty. On the way back she reads her own arrows and gets you home. The ground is frozen hard, so they sit where she put them. Check tomorrow.

The Puzzle Swap

A second set of seven comes off the other cereal box: two builders, two trays, a timer.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 7 items

You need: The seven tangram pieces from this morning, A second set cut from another cereal box, 2 trays or baking sheets, 2 sheets of paper, 1 marker, 1 dish towel, An egg timer or the phone timer

  1. Cut the second set with her calling out which piece comes next. She watched at 8:00 and remembers more of the order than you expect.
  2. One set on each tray, sitting opposite each other with the timer between you.
  3. Two minutes on the clock. Build a picture on your tray without showing her while she builds one on hers.
  4. Slide your tray alongside hers with your picture still standing on it. She clears her own tray and copies yours piece by piece. Set the timer again.
  5. She will get stuck. Let her pick her tray up and turn it round rather than point at the piece she needs.
  6. One round from memory, three pieces only. Build a small shape, give her a slow count of five, drop the dish towel over it and let her go. Three she can hold in her head at this age. Asking for seven ends the afternoon.
  7. Let her set the timer for the last round, then tip both sets into one pile and build one enormous animal.

💡Rebuilding someone else's picture is harder than making your own, and she will say so. Tell her you find it harder too.

The Big Book of Little Days · January · Week 4Day 22 · afternoon →
Finished result d22-result.png
✨ Afternoon alternatives
  • One set only, taking turns to build on the same tray.
  • Solve the four outline cards and stop there.
  • Cut a third set and mail one piece to a grandparent.
  • Draw round every piece on one sheet and color them in.
🌳 Out again · pick one
  • Meet a friend at the park, and take the outline cards
  • The park on your own if nobody is free
  • A café, with the tangram envelope in your bag
  • The short loop past this morning's arrows
  • The big supermarket, and let her find seven of something
Day 22 · For the grown-up The Seven Pieces · Friday, January 22
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 7 months and reaching across his own body now. Sit him near the table with a cardboard tube, then set a second past his right shoulder so he has to swing an arm over for it. He ends up with one in each hand, passing them back and forth. On the walk, carrier facing out, and the crows are the loudest thing he hears all morning.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

Give him a baking sheet of his own on the floor and one wooden spoon. At 7 months he babbles in long runs of bababa and dadada with the shape of sentences in them, so answer him. Wait for the pause, say something back, wait again. He takes the turn.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Sharing and turn-taking are different skills, and one is much easier.

Azlyn will hand you a tangram piece when you say your turn and refuse to hand over the same piece when you say share it. Turn-taking has a shape she can hold in her head. It comes back, and something outside her decides when: a timer, the end of a round, a count. Sharing asks her to give a thing up now with no visible return, and most three-year-olds manage the first a year or more before the second. You already put a timer or a count on it, so the return is something she can hear coming, and the piece leaves her hand.

⚠️

Safety: Seven small card pieces and a 7-month-old who mouths everything do not go together. Build on the table, sweep before you put Kreston down, and count the pieces back into the envelope every time. The scissors are adult only and go back up out of reach between cuts, not onto the table where she is working.

Drawing It Onto the Card

  1. Give her the card blank side up and ask for a drawing that goes to the edges. Big shapes, heavy color, no white left. A photo does the same job if she is not in the mood.
  2. Sit and draw your own beside her without commenting on hers.
  3. Tell her what happens at 9:15: you cut it into pieces. Let her add anything she wants first.

The Jigsaw with Words on the Back

⏱️ 60 min🧰 7 items

You need: 2 sheets of cereal-box card, Her drawing, or a printed photo, 1 glue stick, Scissors (adult only), 1 permanent marker, 1 freezer bag or envelope for storage, 1 tray to build on

  1. Glue the drawing onto the second sheet and press it under a heavy book for ten minutes.
  2. While it presses, write ten things you love about her on the back of an envelope. Specific ones. You hold the door open for Kreston beats you are kind.
  3. Turn the card face down and draw ten chunky pieces on it in marker. Fat lobes, nothing thinner than her finger. Write one of your ten inside each.
  4. Cut along the lines with her holding the card steady. The scissors go back on the shelf as the last piece comes free.
  5. Jumble the pieces picture side up on the tray and let her build it. Hand her the edges and wait to be asked about the middle.
  6. Turn the puzzle over one piece at a time and read what is on the back. All ten, including the ones she talks over.

💡Cut the pieces bigger than looks right. A puzzle she can finish gets built forty times. One that beats her goes in the drawer by Tuesday.

🌳 OUTSIDE

The Winter Bird Match

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Sketch three birds on a scrap of paper before you go, whichever three turn up in January: a crow, a robin, a fat pigeon. Give her a crayon to tick each one off. The hedges are empty, so they show up from a long way off. Home when all three are ticked, or when her hands get cold.

One Piece Each

Five big pieces go out to five people, and the picture arrives when the last comes back.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 5 items

You need: 1 sheet of card, cut into 5 large pieces, Crayons, 1 marker, 5 envelopes or paper bags, Masking tape

  1. Cut one sheet of card into five big pieces with curvy edges. Write a name on the back of each: you, Joseph, Azlyn, Kreston, and a grandparent or the teddy.
  2. Let her hand them out. She reads the names off the backs by shape.
  3. Each person takes their piece away and decorates it. Nobody looks at anybody else's. Kreston's is ten seconds of your hand round his on a fat crayon.
  4. Post each piece into its envelope and seal it.
  5. Collect what you can before you leave for the aquarium at 2:30. She does the asking, and somebody needs chasing twice.
  6. The rest come back at dinner. Build it on the table with everybody there, tape the joins and hang it where she eats breakfast.
  7. Let her point out whose is whose, and say one thing you like about each.

💡Do not tidy anyone's piece, including Kreston's. Five different hands is the picture.

🌳 Out again · pick one
  • The aquarium, the week's big outing, and the dark rooms suit Kreston
  • Indoor playground if the aquarium line is a Saturday one
  • The pet store, for fish at a tenth of the price
  • A walk to water, a river or a pond, and count what moves in it
  • Home, blankets, and the jigsaw on its tray at table height
Day 23 · For the grown-up The Puzzle That Says Something · Saturday, January 23
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 7 months and passing things hand to hand. Give him two cardboard tubes while Azlyn cuts: he takes the second with the empty hand, then moves the first across to free it up. That handover is new this month. Keep card offcuts and the open glue stick away from him.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

The aquarium is built for a 7-month-old. Dark walls, lit tanks, slow-moving things at his eye height in the carrier. His long-distance vision is close to yours now, so he follows one fish across a tank. Twenty-five minutes, then out before the noise stacks up.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Being told what someone loves about you is different from being praised.

Good girl and well done are verdicts. They land on a performance, and the next performance has to earn them again. The ten things on the back of those pieces describe her instead, and she has to do nothing to keep them true. She holds the door for Kreston. She sings to herself in the bath. Nothing on that list can be failed. Children who hear a running verdict on their effort get more careful about trying things they might lose at, and children who hear themselves described build a steadier picture of who they are. The puzzle puts it in her hands.

⚠️

Safety: Ten jigsaw pieces and a 7-month-old on the floor means the tray stays at table height and the count goes back in the bag every time. Glue sticks come apart in a mouth, so the lid goes on and the stick goes up whenever you leave the table. Crayons snap into mouth-sized pieces, so keep your hand round Kreston's for his ten seconds and put the crayon straight back in the box. The scissors are adult only.

Closing the Boxes

You need: the six containers · six small treasures · 1 tray.

  1. The six lidded containers you lined up last night are the morning's puzzle. Lay them out on the table with a treasure beside each. Let her look inside and handle the lids.
  2. She drops a treasure in and you shut them together. Name each closing out loud: screw, clip, zip, tape, knot, band.
  3. Push the tray into the middle of the table and leave it shut until 9:15.

Six Ways to Open a Thing

⏱️ 60 min🧰 8 items

You need: 1 plastic screw-lid jar, 1 clip-lid tub, 1 ziplock bag, 1 shoebox taped shut with masking tape, 1 bag tied with string, 1 tub held shut with an elastic band, 6 small treasures inside: stickers, raisins, a small toy, 1 tray

  1. Put the tray in front of her and sit on your hands. She picks the order and keeps what she gets out.
  2. Count to twenty before you offer anything, then offer a word and not a hand: turning, or find the corner.
  3. The screw lid is hardest, because two hands go opposite ways at once. If she is stuck, she holds the lid still and turns the jar.
  4. The knotted string will beat her. Loosen it to one loop and hand it back so the last pull is hers.
  5. When all six are open, count the treasures. Shut them again, and she picks which fastening goes on which.
  6. Now she loads them and hands you the tray. Struggle out loud with the elastic band.

💡Say what her hands are doing. You are pushing and turning at the same time. She gets words for a thing she worked out.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

The Gate Latch Walk

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Walk the street and try every fastening you are allowed to touch. The park gate with the drop bolt, the churchyard latch, your back gate, the catch on the recycling bin, the brake on the stroller. Cold metal takes a firmer hand than a plastic lid.

The Wall She Fits Through

A flattened box stands between two chairs with a hole in it, and the only way across is through.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: 1 large flattened cardboard box, 1 permanent marker, 1 craft knife or heavy scissors (adult only), 2 dining chairs, Packing tape, 1 blanket for the floor

  1. Spread the blanket, lay the box flat and draw round her while she lies on it, arms out. Leave that outline uncut, because it is the last hole of the afternoon.
  2. Cut a dinner-plate circle high in the panel while she stands back, and put the knife away before the box goes upright.
  3. Tape the box between the chair backs so it stands like a wall, blanket underneath.
  4. She goes through the circle first. Starting easy is why she is still going at the fourth.
  5. Take the box down, cut a new hole, stand it back up. A tall slot, a mail slot low down she crosses on her belly, one cut too small on purpose. Knife away before it goes up.
  6. Let her name each shape and work out her own way through. She tries head-first twice before discovering feet.
  7. Her own outline comes last, and cutting it takes the middle out of the wall. She walks through the shape of herself and the wall goes with her.

💡Cut the next hole while she is still enjoying the last. The activity dies the moment she stands and watches you measure.

The Big Book of Little Days · January · Week 4Day 24 · afternoon →

✨ Afternoon alternatives
  • One hole, one box, and she goes through it forty times.
  • Crawl tunnel out of two chairs and a blanket instead.
  • Post small toys through a slot in a shoebox lid and shake them out.
🌳 Out again · pick one
  • A playground you have never been to, and let her lead once you are there
  • Your usual park, if the new one is a parking lot with a swing
  • The woods loop, for gates, stiles and cold mud
  • A drive to somewhere with a view, staying in the warm car
Day 24 · For the grown-up Getting It Open · Sunday, January 24
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 7 months. Seal something rattly inside a clip-lid tub and hand it over. He cannot open it, so he shakes it, bangs it and passes it hand to hand. Hide a toy under a dish towel while he watches, and the first time he pulls it off he will look up at you.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

Lie him on the blanket on the far side of the wall so Azlyn comes through and lands next to him. A face appearing where a wall was is peekaboo, and at 7 months nothing is funnier. At the playground, a bucket swing with your hand on him, two or three pushes and out.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Puzzles build a skill that has nothing to do with puzzles.

Six lids is a morning of Azlyn trying a thing, failing, and trying a different thing. That loop is the skill and it travels. Researchers who follow children into school find that staying with a hard task predicts school outcomes as strongly as anything they can measure at four. A closed container is a good place to practice, because the problem is honest: the lid is off or it is not, no adult decides whether she did well, and the treasure pays out the second she solves it. She sets her own difficulty, picking which one to attack next. You keep your hands still and she banks another minute.

⚠️

Safety: Elastic bands, raisins and a ziplock bag are hazards for a 7-month-old. Work at the table, count the six treasures in and out, and pick the band up the moment it comes off. The craft knife is adult only and goes out of reach between every cut, not onto the arm of the sofa. Sit a bag of shopping on each chair seat to hold them down, stay beside her while she goes through, and tape the box so it pulls loose rather than dragging a chair over on her. Never leave Kreston beside the standing box wall on his own.

Filling the Tray

You need: 1 tray · the run of the house · 1 dish towel.

  1. Hand her the tray and send her round the house for eight things bigger than her fist. You veto nothing that fits the rule.
  2. Lay them out in two rows of four and name each one out loud. Let her shuffle them until it looks right to her.
  3. Cover the tray with the dish towel and leave it on the table. Say nothing about what happens next.

What's Missing from the Tray

⏱️ 60 min🧰 4 items

You need: 1 tray, 8–10 household objects bigger than her fist: mug, wooden spoon, hairbrush, sock, apple, board book, sponge, shoe, 1 dish towel to cover the tray, Paper and a pencil for keeping score

  1. Uncover the tray and name all eight, pointing at each. Give her a slow count of ten.
  2. Cover it. She turns round or shuts her eyes. Take one object off and sit on it.
  3. Uncover and let her name what has gone. If she stalls, name the ones still there and let her hear the gap.
  4. Drop to six objects if eight is too many, go up to ten when eight stops being work.
  5. Swap over. She takes one while you look away, and you work it out loud: sock, apple, book, and the spoon was next to the book.
  6. Keep score in tally marks, hers and yours, and leave the tray out so she can run it on whoever walks in.

💡Let her win most of them. A three-year-old who is getting them right stays at the table. One stretched every round leaves after four rounds.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

She Leads the Way Home

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Walk ten minutes out from the door, taking three or four turns, then hand the job over: she gets you home. Name what you pass on the way out, the red door, the mailbox, the dog behind the fence. January sun sits low enough to change how the street looks coming back, so expect one wrong turn and let her walk into it.

The Pairs She Draws Herself

Sixteen blank cards, eight drawings done twice, and a memory game she made herself.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 4 items

You need: Card offcuts cut into 16 palm-sized cards, Crayons, 1 marker, 1 shoebox lid to keep them in

  1. Lay the sixteen cards out blank side up and tell her the job: eight things, each drawn twice, so every card has a twin.
  2. Start her off. Draw a red circle on one card, hand her the second, and let her copy it. Wobbly copies are fine.
  3. She picks the other seven. A fish, a sun, a spot, whatever comes. Draw one of each pair yourself if her hand gets tired.
  4. Go over the faint crayon lines in marker so they read from across the table.
  5. Play with four pairs first. Eight cards face down in two rows, turn two over, and put them back the same way up in the same place if they do not match.
  6. Add pairs as she holds it. Twelve cards, then all sixteen. Stop adding the round before she starts guessing at random.
  7. Everything goes in the shoebox lid and stays out for 4:15. She plays it again on her own with the cards face up.

💡Put the cards back in the exact spot they came from. Half of this game is her remembering where.

  • Match the pairs face up as a sorting game and skip the memory part.
  • Draw the eight things on paper instead and cut them out together.
  • Play snap with the finished cards instead of pairs.
🌳 Out again · pick one
  • Green space and a ball, the Monday slot, and a ball is warmer than a bench
  • The neighborhood park if the grass is under water
  • A walk with one job: find five things you saw this morning
  • The big field, for running in a straight line until she stops
  • Round the block on the scooter while the light holds
Day 25 · For the grown-up The Memory Tray · Monday, January 25
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 7 months and working on Azlyn's question: does a thing still exist when nobody can see it. Play peekaboo with the dish towel over your face, then over a toy. Give him the wooden spoon off the tray and let him drop it from the high chair. He is checking that it lands every time, and it does.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

Give him two of anything identical, two wooden spoons or two cups, one for each hand. At 7 months he holds both and studies them, and the banging-together stage is weeks off. On the grass, sit him on a folded blanket where he can watch the ball go past. He turns his whole body after it.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Working memory is the thing she is building.

The tray game runs on the same system Azlyn uses to follow you round the house: working memory, the part that holds a few things in mind while doing something with them. At three she can hold two or three items, which is why go upstairs, get your socks and bring down the blue cup arrives as one item, and it is seldom the right one. The tray gives the same system a workout she volunteered for. Eight objects sit above her ceiling, so she leans on the layout and the gap in the rows, which is memory strategy showing up early.

⚠️

Safety: Count the sixteen cards into the shoebox lid and out of it every time, and keep the tray of objects up at table height while Kreston is on the floor. Sweep under the table before he goes down. Crayons snap into mouth-sized pieces, so the broken halves go in the trash as they happen, and the wooden spoon he drops off the high chair is the only thing off that tray he gets.

The Basket of Everything

You need: the full basket · 4 bowls or paper bags · masking tape and a marker.

  1. The laundry basket you filled last night holds twenty or thirty of the house's odds and ends. Tip it out on the floor and sit in the pile with her. Half of it she has not seen for weeks and she will greet all of it.
  2. Ask her to put two things together that go together. Take whatever reason she gives, including they are both Kreston's. Three or four times.
  3. Line the four bowls up beside the pile and say nothing about what goes in them. The sorting starts at 9:15.

The main event · 9:15–10:15 AM

Sorting It Twice

⏱️ 60 min🧰 4 items

You need: 1 basket of 20–30 mixed household objects and toys, 4 bowls or paper bags, Paper and a marker for labels, Masking tape

  1. Four bowls, four colors. Tape a colored scrap to each or write the color word on it. She sorts the whole pile, and the two-color ones are hers to call.
  2. Walk her along the four bowls and count each one out loud. Announce the winner.
  3. Tip the lot back into one pile.
  4. Same objects, new rule: things that need two hands, things that fit in one. Two bowls. She will complain about starting again, then beat her own time.
  5. Third round is hers. She sorts by a rule she keeps secret and you work it out from what lands in each bowl. Guess wrong twice before you get there.
  6. Her rule will be things I like and things I do not. Both count. Write it on the paper, read it back and tape it to the bowl.

💡The moment worth waiting for is the second sort, when a red spoon that was a red thing an hour ago becomes a two-hands thing. Say so out loud.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

Two Bags, One Rule

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Two paper bags and one rule set at the front gate: things that came off a tree in the left bag, things that never did in the right. Late January hands over brown leaves, bare twigs, a seed head, a bottle cap, gravel. The arguments are the good part. Ten minutes of collecting is plenty in this cold.

Outdoors d26-outside.png

Every Lid Has a Box

The kitchen floor gets the version with a real result, and by six she has fixed two things you meant to fix in November.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 5 items

You need: All the tupperware boxes and lids, The silverware drawer, knives removed first, 1 dish towel, 1 dishpan, Masking tape and a marker for labeling shelves

  1. Take every knife and skewer out of the drawer and onto the top of the fridge before she comes into the kitchen.
  2. Tip all the tupperware onto the floor. Lids in one heap, boxes in another, three feet apart.
  3. She matches. Hand her the three most obvious, then stand back. A lid that almost fits is the best part of the job.
  4. Any box with no lid goes in the dishpan, out of the house or into the craft pile. She makes the call.
  5. Stack the matched boxes biggest at the bottom and put them back on the shelf. Tape a label on the shelf edge and let her say what to write.
  6. Now the drawer. Tip it onto the dish towel and let her sort each piece back into its slot: forks, spoons, teaspoons, a bowl for the odd stuff.
  7. Leave the drawer open. She checks her own work at 4:00 when she does the forks.

💡Do not re-sort behind her tonight. She walks past that drawer forty times this week, and every time she opens it she sees something she got right.

  • The lids only, and stop when the tupperware is done.
  • Sort the toy basket into two boxes, one of them for the thrift store.
  • Pair the shoes by the front door, all facing the same way.
🌳 Out again · pick one
  • Swimming, the Tuesday anchor, and the fourth of the year
  • The indoor play center if the pool is shut
  • A warm café and a window seat, if nobody has it in them
  • Home, a warm bath instead, and an extra book at five
Day 26 · For the grown-up Two Ways to Sort · Tuesday, January 26
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 7 months. Give him his own bowl with two objects too big to swallow and watch what he does. He takes them out and does not put them back, because putting things into a container comes around nine months. Today he empties, you refill, and he thinks that is the game.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He comes too if he is up for it. At 7 months he sits supported in the water and splashes with intent. The pool hall throws his own voice back at him, so he shouts at the ceiling and waits to hear it again. Hold him chest to chest at first, twenty minutes and out before he cools.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Classification is quiet, invisible math.

Before Azlyn can count six forks she has to decide what a fork is and that these six are all one kind of thing. Sorting is where that gets settled. Every bowl she fills is a set, every argument about the two-color ones is her testing where the edge of a category sits, and number is built on top of that. The second sort does something further. Running a new rule over the same objects, color one hour and size the next, is the flexible half of the job, and it is harder than the first sort. You have her pairing socks and sorting silverware already. Same task, real result.

⚠️

Safety: Knives, skewers and anything with a point come out of the drawer before she is in the room and stay out until it goes back. Small sorted objects stay off the floor while Kreston is down there, and the basket goes up on the table between rounds. Never leave the drawer open at her height with the sharp things still in it. Swimming this afternoon. Both children stay within arm's reach in the water at all times, and no float or seat is a substitute for your hands.

Opening activity · 8:00–9:00 AM

Choosing the Secret Objects

You need: 1 pillowcase or tote bag · a wander round the house · 1 tray.

  1. Send her round for things that feel different, one out of every room. Rough, cold, furry, prickly, smooth.
  2. Feel each one before it goes in, hands only and eyes on the ceiling. Give her three words for it and ask for three back.
  3. Mail them all into the pillowcase and stand it where she can see it and not reach in. She will try anyway.

🎨 MAKE
The main event · 9:15–10:15 AM

The Bag You Can't See Into

⏱️ 60 min🧰 3 items

You need: 1 pillowcase or tote bag, 8–10 objects with different textures, all bigger than a fist: orange, hairbrush, scrubbing brush, wooden spoon, washcloth, shoe, mug, bath sponge, 1 tray to lay the guessed ones on

  1. Sit opposite each other with the bag between you. One rule: hand goes in, eyes stay out.
  2. Whoever's turn it is finds one object and says three things about it before anybody guesses. Hard, cold, round.
  3. Go first so she hears what three things sounds like. Take your time and be wrong at the end.
  4. Her turn. She will blurt the answer out, at least twice. Ask for one more thing and let her hold it while she thinks.
  5. Objects come out onto the tray as they are named. When the bag is empty, cover it and see how many she can list.
  6. Last round the other way: you describe one from memory, hands on the table, and she finds it in the bag by feel.

💡Give her the words she is missing while her hand is on the object. Bumpy and ridged and cold at one end land now and vanish later.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

Eyes Shut, Five Sounds

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Stop on the path, both shut your eyes, and count five sounds off on her fingers. There are no leaves this week so sound carries: a crow, a car, a dog, a plane, your own boots on the grit. Do it again by a road and behind a hedge, and ask which was louder. She points at the road with her eyes still shut.

Outdoors d27-outside.png

Picture Clues

Six drawings, taped round the house, each sending her to where the next one waits.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 5 items

You need: Paper cut into 6 cards, Crayons, Masking tape, 1 small prize: a cookie or a sticker, 1 teddy to hide

  1. Hide teddy first with the prize under him, somewhere she walks past twenty times a day.
  2. Draw six clues, one per card: the bath, the fridge, her boots, the sofa, the kitchen trash can, and last of all teddy's spot. Rough drawings are fine.
  3. Tape clue one where she will start. Every card sends her to the place drawn on it, where the next waits.
  4. Walk it with her and carry nothing. She holds the card, she decides where the drawing means, she gets to be wrong about the fridge.
  5. She finds teddy, gets the prize and eats it standing up in the hall.
  6. Now she hides teddy and draws your six clues. No help with the drawings, however long they take.
  7. Follow her clues as drawn, including the one that makes no sense. Ask what it is and take the answer she gives.

💡She will want to tell you where teddy is about four clues in. Ask her to whisper it to the wall and go on hunting. Holding a secret for ten minutes is work.

  • Hot and cold, called out loud, with no cards at all.
  • Hide the same object ten times and get faster each round.
  • Draw a map of the downstairs and mark an X on it.

  • Indoor playground with the quiet session, if the big one is full of the school-pickup crowd

  • The store, and let her carry one thing and pay for it
  • A friend's house with the mystery bag in your coat pocket
Day 27 · For the grown-up Describe It First · Wednesday, January 27
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 7 months and his mouth is still his best instrument for finding out what a thing is. Give him a washcloth, a wooden spoon and a silicone spatula, one at a time. Put words on each while he works it over. Keep the bath sponge in the bag and out of his reach, because it comes apart in bits.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

The baby area at the play center is his. Sit him in the ball pit shallows with a hand on his back, because at 7 months he sits well but tips at speed. Mirrors at his level beat any of the toys. Twenty minutes, then out to somewhere quieter.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Describing before guessing is the whole skill.

Guessing is fast and closes the thinking down. Describing keeps it open and costs her more, because she has to find words for weight, temperature, texture and shape while her hand is the only thing telling her anything. Every one of those words is a category she can carry to the next object. Teachers call this attribute language, and children with plenty of it find it easier later to explain how they got to an answer, which is most of what school asks them for. The rule you set at the top, three things before anybody guesses, is what does the work.

⚠️

Safety: The bath sponge comes apart in bits, so it goes back in the bag between turns and the bag stays off the floor. Hide the cookie somewhere Kreston cannot get to, and let Azlyn eat it before you put him down. Press the tape ends flat on every clue you stick up at his height, and pull them all off the walls once the hunt is over.

Opening activity · 8:00–9:00 AM

Cutting the Maze Walls

You need: cereal-box card · scissors (adult only) · 1 baking tray · masking tape.

  1. Cut the card into strips two fingers wide. She counts them into a pile as they come off, and you want about fifteen.
  2. Fold each strip along its length so it stands on its own edge. Let her fold all fifteen and leave the crooked ones crooked.
  3. Stand a few loose in the baking tray and let her shove them round with one finger. Nothing gets taped down until 9:15.
Materials, laid out d28-materials.png

🎨 MAKE
The main event · 9:15–10:15 AM

The Maze in a Tray

⏱️ 60 min🧰 6 items

You need: 1 baking tray or shallow box lid, Cereal-box card cut into strips, 1 roll masking tape, Scissors (adult only), 1 ping-pong ball, or a tight ball of foil, 1 marker

  1. Draw the route on paper first. Start at one corner, finish at the other, four turns between. Mark three dead ends and let her put an X on each.
  2. Tape the first walls into the tray along the route you drew, gaps wide enough for the ball.
  3. Build in the three dead ends. Say nothing about them at all.
  4. Give her the ball and let her tilt. She will hit the first dead end inside ten seconds and look up at you. Look back and keep quiet.
  5. Once she has all three worked out, hand her the tape and tell her the maze is hers to change. She will open the dead ends up.
  6. Last run on the floor, tray held in two hands, standing over it. Time her, then let her time you and be slower.

💡Keep the walls low enough to see over. She has to watch the ball go the wrong way to know it went wrong, and a tall wall turns it into luck.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

She Picks Every Turning

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Out the front door and every junction is hers. She calls left or right, you walk it, no steering and no hints. Turn back at twenty minutes and let her get you home. Some of her turns are dead ends, somebody's driveway or a fence, and those are the good ones. The cold sits in her hands this week, so mittens on.

Outdoors d28-outside.png

The Maze You Walk

Tape on the floor, cushions for corners, teddy at the finish, and this time the thing going through the maze is her.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 5 items

You need: 2 rolls masking tape, 4 sofa cushions, 2 dining chairs, 1 teddy for the end, Paper and a marker to draw the plan first

  1. Draw the plan together on paper. She can copy the tray maze or invent a new one, but three dead ends go on it first.
  2. Clear one room end to end. Lay the tape two lines at a time so she watches a corridor appear rather than a finished puzzle.
  3. Cushions and chair legs go on the corners where tape on the floor stops reading as a wall.
  4. Teddy waits at the finish. She starts on the taped X by the door.
  5. First run she walks it. Second run on all fours, third on tiptoe, fourth carrying teddy back the other way without touching a wall.
  6. Hand her the tape and let her turn one dead end into a door.
  7. Leave it down for the evening and make everybody walk it to get to dinner, including whoever comes in at six.

💡Run it once yourself, out loud, saying what you think at each turn. That is a wall, so I am going back to the last corner. She takes the words for her next run.
