Day 28 · For the grown-up Dead Ends · Thursday, January 28
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 7 months. The ping-pong ball and the foil stay up on the table, so give him something too big to swallow: a soccer ball, or a rolled-up towel. Roll it across him at walking pace so he follows it over his own midline and reaches across. He may push himself backwards trying and end up under the sofa, which is how a lot of babies move first.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

Put him at the finish next to teddy, so Azlyn's arrival is the reward for the pair of them. He is 7 months and picking at edges with his fingers, so press the tape ends flat and pull up anything that has lifted. In the post office line, hand him something to hold before he decides for himself.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Dead ends are the point of a maze.

A maze with no wrong turns in it is a corridor. The three dead ends make Azlyn stop, look at where she has got to, decide the route was wrong and go back. That is a different job from pushing harder at the same thing. Psychologists call dropping a plan that is not working cognitive flexibility, and three is about when it arrives. Her first move at a dead end will be to shove the ball into the wall again. Wait. The second thing she tries is the one worth having, and you gave her a wrong turn she can survive, with nothing riding on it.

⚠️

Safety: The ping-pong ball and any foil balls or dried beans in the tray are a choking hazard for Kreston. Build at table height, count the ball back in at the end of every run, and sweep before he goes down on the floor. The scissors are adult only and go back up out of reach between cuts.

Day 29
The Animal Coats
The Big Book of Little Days · January · Week 4Day 28 · for the grown-up
January · Week 5

Forest Friends 🌲

January 29 – February 4, 2027 · Days 29–35

Azlyn prints four animal coats on Friday morning and builds the animals after lunch, then spends the rest of the week finding places for them to live. A tree up the living room wall on Saturday, a forest floor in a baking tray on Sunday, tracks across the hall on Monday, feeders outside the window on Tuesday, a cave in a cardboard box on Wednesday. Every day inherits the day before it. By Thursday she has a forest in the house and enough of it in her head to tell the whole week back to you through a lit sheet.

February arrives on Monday, and Groundhog Day lands on Tuesday the 2nd as a bonus note inside the afternoon: people in America gather round a hole to watch a woodchuck come up and check the weather. It sits an inch from Wednesday's hibernation cave, so the two can talk to each other. The cold does the rest of the work this week. Frost on the grass until the sun comes round the houses, bare branches with every old nest showing, and shadows that run long at eleven in the morning.

🧒 What Azlyn will learn
  • Patterns she can carry on. Spot, spot, stripe down a paper strip, then finishing the row without you.
  • Where forest animals live. Roots, trunk, branches, top, and which animal belongs at which height.
  • Reading evidence. A print, a chewed leaf and a tuft of wool add up to an animal she never saw.
  • Waiting, and holding still on purpose. She fills four feeders on Tuesday and the birds come on Thursday; she hibernates on Wednesday while you count to twenty.
  • Telling the week back. Two tours, a puppet show, and a shadow fox that swells up the sheet as she walks him toward the flashlight.
👶 KRESTON THIS WEEK

Kreston is 7 months this week. He reaches across his body for things set out to one side, passes them from hand to hand, and babbles in long strings that carry the rhythm of sentences and none of the words. He turns 8 months on Friday the 5th, the day after this week ends.

The Big Book of Little Days · JanuaryWeek 5 · opener →
🌍 Around the world Week 5 · read it on Day 29

Japan, Shinrin-yoku 🌲

In Japan, shinrin-yoku means forest bathing, a walk with nothing to achieve. No route, no distance, no finish. You go in among the trees and use your senses: what you can hear, what you can smell, how bark feels under a hand. Japanese doctors send patients out to do it, and the walk counts as treatment.

✨
Try it

Green tea and a rice ball, eaten under a tree with your coats on. Ten minutes of sitting and listening counts as the whole practice.

The Big Book of Little Days · JanuaryWeek 5 · around the world →
Around the world w5-world.png
👩 What you'll learn
  • Patterns are the beginning of algebra
  • Explaining to someone else is how understanding gets locked in
  • Loose parts beat finished toys
  • Evidence and inference, a big idea learnable at three
  • Delayed payoff is a muscle, and this is a gentle way to work it
  • Pretending to sleep is real self-regulation practice
  • Shadows are confusing at three, and the confusion is worth exploring
Did you know

Japan's forestry ministry invented the word shinrin-yoku in 1982, and the name came before any of the science did.

Opening activity · 8:00–9:00 AM

The Stamp Hunt

You need: 1 grocery bag · the recycling · the odds drawer.

  1. Hand her the bag and one job: find things that make a mark. A cork, a fork, a spool of thread, a tube end, a bottle cap.
  2. Press each find into your palm and ask what shape it would leave. Take her guesses without fixing them.
  3. Line the winners along the table edge in the order she wants to use them. That is the plan for 9:15.
Materials, laid out d29-materials.png

Day 29 · The main event The Animal Coats · Friday, January 29

🎨 MAKE
The main event · 9:15–10:15 AM

Printing the Animal Coats

⏱️ 60 min🧰 6 items

You need: Long paper strips cut from a paper bag or the back of wrapping paper, 6, Washable non-toxic poster paint in brown, black, white and orange, 1 saucer or old plate for each color, Cardboard tube ends, 1 cork, 1 fork, 1 crumpled piece of paper towel, 1 wet washcloth in a shallow bowl, Newspaper for the table

  1. Spread the newspaper, lay one strip in front of her the long way, and pour a thin puddle of each color into its own saucer.
  2. Start the fawn. Two spots with the cork, a stripe dragged with the back of the fork, two spots again. Say it as you print: spot, spot, stripe. Hand her the cork on the third repeat.
  3. Raccoon next. Wide dark and pale bands from a tube squashed flat, alternating down the strip like a ringed tail. She takes over after two.
  4. Owl on the third strip: rings from the open end of a tube, rows of them, brown on brown.
  5. Fox on the fourth: orange the whole length with the crumpled paper towel, then a white tip.
  6. Hand her the last two strips with no pattern to follow. Those two are hers, printed however she likes. Lay all six flat to dry, wash hands, then walk the row and ask what comes next on the four you started.

💡Print the first repeat and stop. She finishes the strip. A pattern she completed is one she can read back at you an hour later.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

The Bark Rubbing Walk

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Take paper and a fat crayon with the wrapper peeled off. Rub the crayon on its side over paper held flat against four different trunks. Oak comes out deep and ridged, birch close to smooth, and she feels the difference through the paper before she sees it. January bark holds the wet, so work the sheltered side of each trunk.

Outdoors d29-outside.png
The Big Book of Little Days · January · Week 5Day 29 · main event →
Day 29 · Afternoon The Animal Coats · Friday, January 29
⏱️ 1:00 onward
🎨 MAKE
Second main event · 1:00–2:30 PM

Building the Forest Family

The strips are dry by one o'clock. Wrapped round a cardboard tube and taped, each one stands up on the table by itself.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: The printed strips, Cardboard tubes, 4–6, 1 roll masking tape, Scissors (adult), Card scraps for ears, tails and beaks, 1 permanent marker

  1. Lay the dry strips out and ask which animal each one is. Take her answer even when the raccoon has turned into a zebra.
  2. Wrap the fawn strip round a tube with the pattern facing out and tape the seam on the inside. She holds, you tape.
  3. Cut ears, a tail and a beak from the card scraps. She draws the shape, you cut on her line.
  4. Tape the pieces where she points, including the ears you would have put somewhere else.
  5. Stand each animal on the table as you go so the row grows in front of her.
  6. Write every name on the base in marker. Fox is a name and so is Bibby.
  7. Give them an address: a shelf, a windowsill, the corner of the table. They stay there all week.

💡Tape the seam inside the tube where her fingers cannot find it. A seam she can pick at comes apart by Sunday, and these four have a week of work ahead.

  • Grandparents, or whoever in the family is nearest, and she takes one animal to show them
  • A friend's house, if the Forest Family needs an audience under five

Day 29 · For the grown-up The Animal Coats · Friday, January 29
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 7 months and passes things from hand to hand now. Give him a wooden spoon and a folded washcloth, the second set out to his side so he has to reach across his body for it. He keeps up a running commentary at both of them while Azlyn prints. On the walk, hold his open palm flat against a trunk for a second.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

Keep him off the tape and the tube ends and give him a big offcut of card instead, wider than his own mouth. At 7 months he pulls at paper with both hands and turns it over hunting for the other side. He runs a long string of sound at you while he works, so answer as though he asked you something.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Patterns are the beginning of algebra.

Azlyn printed spot, spot, stripe, spot, spot, stripe down a paper strip this morning, and the work underneath it is what a nine-year-old does with x. A pattern is a rule that holds while the pieces change. Once she can say what comes next on the raccoon strip, she can find the rule in a row of cups, a clapped rhythm or a line of numbers, because one skill sits under all three. Researchers who track early math find pattern work predicts where a child lands later, alongside counting, and it adds something counting does not. You never have to name it. Print the first repeat, hand her the cork, and let her carry the rule to the end.

⚠️

Safety: Kreston is 7 months and everything he reaches goes in his mouth. Corks, tube ends and card scraps go up out of reach the moment you stop watching, on a shelf and not the table edge. Washable non-toxic paint only. The scissors stay with you.

Tearing the Trunk

You need: brown paper bags or a flattened box · masking tape · the cleared wall.

  1. Tear the paper into long ragged strips instead of cutting it. A torn edge looks like bark, and her hands can do it all.
  2. Lay the strips end to end along the floor and stand her beside the line.
  3. Ask where the branches should start. Tape a tab on the wall at that height and leave the pile until 9:15.

The Tree That Fills the Wall

⏱️ 60 min🧰 6 items

You need: Brown paper bags, a flattened cardboard box, or the plain side of wrapping paper, 1 roll masking tape, Scissors (adult), Green paper, newspaper or magazine pages for leaves, 1 permanent marker, The Forest Family animals, or any toy animals

  1. Tape the strips she tore this morning to the cleared wall as a trunk, floor to shoulder height, wider at the bottom. Overlap them until no wall shows.
  2. Add branches from the shorter strips. She decides how many and where, and crooked ones stay crooked.
  3. Tear leaves from the green paper or magazine pages and tape them along the branches in handfuls.
  4. Draw a line along the baseboard and run roots below it. That line is the ground.
  5. Sort the animals. Ask where each one lives: roots, trunk, branches, top. Tape a card shelf at that height and stand it there.
  6. Write the four layers up the wall in marker: roots, trunk, branches, top. Read them out with her, bottom up.

💡Build it at her height. A tree she can reach the top of is one she keeps adding to all week, and the ceiling end is yours.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

Choosing Her Tree

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Walk the route and let her pick one tree. She has to give a reason, and any reason counts. Put both arms round the trunk to see whether they meet, then count the big branches. Photograph her against it today.

The Forest Tour

She knows where every animal on that wall lives. This afternoon she says it out loud to an audience that cannot get up and leave.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: The wall tree, 1 flashlight, 1 cardboard tube, for a megaphone, Paper scraps and 1 crayon, for tickets, Your phone, to record one tour for Joseph, A chair each for the teddies, and a cushion on the floor for Kreston

  1. Set the chairs in a row facing the tree with a teddy in every one. Kreston sits at the end, propped against the cushion.
  2. Make tickets. She scribbles on the paper scraps and hands one to every seat, Kreston included.
  3. Give her the tube and the flashlight. The tube is her voice and the flashlight is her pointer.
  4. Take a seat and be the audience. Who lives at the top. Why does nobody live in the roots. What happens up there when it rains.
  5. Let her be wrong. Owls in the roots is a claim, and a claim beats a correct answer copied off you.
  6. Record one tour start to finish with no retakes. Joseph gets it tonight.
  7. Swap over. You give the tour, and she corrects you before you finish the first sentence.

💡Ask for the tour twice with an hour in between. The second runs longer and adds something she worked out in the gap.

  • Give the whole tour to Joseph on a video call.
🌳 Out again · pick one
  • The botanical garden, greenhouse first if the wind is up
  • A garden center with an indoor plant section, the same trees in miniature
  • The park with the biggest trees you know, for the shapes of them bare
  • A churchyard or an arboretum, both good for old trunks in winter
  • A café near the garden and a hot chocolate on the way home
Day 30 · For the grown-up The Tree on the Wall · Saturday, January 30
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 7 months and tracks Azlyn across a room now. Lay him on his back under the wall tree to look up at the leaves. Tape one green paper leaf at the height of his hand, off to one side so he has to reach across his body for it. He crumples it and passes it over.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

At 7 months the wet warm air of the greenhouse, the smell and the change in sound as the door shuts all land at once, and he goes still and stares. Carry him facing out and stop at three plants, his hand under yours on one big rubbery leaf. Back home he props against a cushion at the end of the row.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Explaining to someone else is how understanding gets locked in.

Azlyn giving the tour is doing harder work than Azlyn being told. To explain the tree she has to put the parts in an order, find words for the joins, and run into the bits she does not have. Researchers call it self-explanation, and children who talk their way through a problem hold on to it longer than children who watched a demonstration. Her audience does not need to follow a word. Kreston and three teddies do the job as well as an adult, because the value sits in the telling. Ask one real question at the end and let the silence run while she hunts for the answer.

⚠️

Safety: Kreston sits on the floor against a cushion for the tour and never on a dining chair. At 7 months he goes over sideways with no warning. The leaf taped at his height and every loose end of masking tape come away the moment you stop watching, because both go straight to his mouth. The scissors stay with you, up on a shelf between cuts.

The Odds and Ends Hunt

You need: the bowl of odds and ends · 1 baking tray · 1 jar lid.

  1. Tip the bowl into the middle of the table and let her go through it.
  2. Give her three words: log, rock, leaf. Ask which things in the pile could be each. A cork can be a log, a bottle cap a rock.
  3. Set the jar lid in the middle of the empty tray and tell her it is the pond. Nothing else goes in until 9:15.

The Forest Floor Tray

⏱️ 60 min🧰 6 items

You need: 1 baking tray or a large shallow box lid, Soil, sand or torn brown paper for the ground, Corks, clothespins, bottle caps, cotton balls, fabric scraps, 1 jar lid for the pond, Small stones and twigs from the yard, 1 pitcher of water

  1. Spread the ground first: soil, sand, or brown paper torn small. Her hands do it. Sweep at the end.
  2. Press the jar lid in and let her pour water from the pitcher. Refill it rather than telling her to go careful.
  3. Lay the corks as fallen logs and the clothespins as branches. Stand the twigs up as trees, pushed in or taped to the tray edge.
  4. Build one hollow under a cork to sleep in, and one heap of cotton balls for a nest.
  5. Ring the pond with the small stones. Ask what is missing and put in whatever she names.
  6. Leave one corner bare. You collect for it at 10:30 and fill it after lunch, so tell her that now.

💡Give her the whole bowl, not a chosen handful. Deciding which cork is a log is the part she came for.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

What's Under the Leaves

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Take a paper bag and turn over the leaf litter at the bottom of a hedge. The underneath of January is wet, dark and busy: leaves gone to skeleton, a pill bug, an empty snail shell, twigs going soft. Lift one stone, look, and put it back as you found it. Fill the bag with moss, bark and four good twigs.

Moving the Animals In

The collecting bag has sat by the front door since eleven. Empty it into the bare corner of the tray, and the Forest Family moves in on top.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: The forest floor tray, The collecting bag from this morning, The Forest Family animals, or any toy animals, 1 roll masking tape, 1 spray bottle, or a spoon and a cup of water, for rain, 1 permanent marker for name labels

  1. Tip the bag onto newspaper beside the tray and go through it piece by piece. She decides what goes in.
  2. Press the moss down as ground cover and lean the bark against a cork for a roof.
  3. Bring the animals over one at a time. Each one needs somewhere to sleep and she picks the spot.
  4. Write each name on masking tape and stick it on the tray edge below that animal.
  5. Make it rain, one squeeze of the spray bottle or a spoonful tipped from a height. Watch where it runs and who chose a bad spot.
  6. Move whoever got wet. Ask why the new place is drier and take her reasoning as it comes.
  7. Lift the tray onto the table when she has finished. It comes down again tomorrow.

💡Rain is the best thing here and she will ask for it eleven times. Set the number before you start, three rains, and hold the line, or the tray is soup by two.

  • The same hedge again with a flashlight as the light goes

Day 31 · For the grown-up The Forest Floor · Sunday, January 31
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 7 months and everything goes to his mouth. Keep him clear of the tray and give him a bowl of his own with a wooden spoon and a folded washcloth in it. On the walk, hold one big dry leaf out for him to grab. He gets it to his mouth in under a second, so keep hold of your half.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He comes on the hunt in the carrier facing out with a hat over his ears. Stop three times and hold him up to touch a wall, a wet leaf, a cold gate. Name each one as his hand lands. At 7 months he answers every name with a run of sound, so leave him the gap to put it in.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Loose parts beat finished toys.

A bowl of corks, clothespins and bottle caps puts a decision in front of Azlyn on every piece she picks up. The cork has to become a log, and she makes it one. Architects and playworkers call these loose parts: the more a material can turn into, the longer a child stays with it and the more she says. A toy fox stays a fox for as long as you own it. Her cork is a log, then a seat, then a bear, and each change is a thought she had. Keep a bowl of them where she can reach and top it up from the recycling.

⚠️

Safety: Small stones, corks and bottle caps sit at mouth height for a 7-month-old. The tray lives on the table between sessions and never on the floor while Kreston is loose in the room. Soil and leaf litter mean hands washed before the snack. Tip the pond out when she has finished.

The Four Feet

You need: paper · 1 crayon · the 2 paw stamps · one shut door.

  1. Draw four feet on one sheet: a bird's, a duck's, a grown-up's, and a paw with four toes. Draw them rough; she will still read them.
  2. Ask whose is whose and take the wrong answers without fixing them. Then ask what each foot is good at. Gripping, swimming, walking, digging.
  3. Press one paw stamp onto the paper dry so she meets the shape before the trail. Something came through the house in the night, and that door stays shut until 9:15.

The Track Trail

⏱️ 60 min🧰 6 items

You need: All-purpose flour, 2 cups, in a sieve or a small bowl, 2 paw shapes cut from a sponge or thick card, Dark paper or a dark towel for the prints to show up on, 3 clues: a chewed leaf, a tuft of wool, a few crumbs, 1 hidden animal from the Forest Family, or any toy animal, 1 dustpan and brush

  1. The flour trail you laid last night waits behind the shut door. Open it and stand back. Let her look before anybody says a word.
  2. Follow it from the start on hands and knees. Count the prints out loud and let her take over.
  3. Stop at every clue and ask the same question: what does this tell us. A chewed leaf says it eats plants, a tuft of wool says it is furry, crumbs say it went past the trash can.
  4. Find the animal at the end. She lifts whatever it is hiding under and says the name.
  5. Now walk it backwards, animal to door, and ask which way it was going. This is the hard part.
  6. Sweep up together. Keep half a cup of flour back for after lunch.

💡Do not tell her who it was at the start. Guessing wrong for ten minutes and finding out at the end is the whole activity.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

Footprints in the Frost

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Early February holds frost on grass and car roofs until the sun comes round, and a mild morning gives you soft mud instead, which takes a print better. Walk the shaded side of the street and read what crossed it in the night: a cat's prints along a wall, bird feet in a puddle, her own boots on white grass. Send her across the lawn, then turn her round to see what she left.

Laying a Trail for Joseph

Joseph walks in at six tonight with no idea there is anything on the floor. Azlyn spends the afternoon making sure there is.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: The paw stamps and the flour, Paper and crayons for arrow cards, 1 roll masking tape, One thing to hide at the end, chosen by her, 1 flashlight, 1 dustpan and brush

  1. Walk the route with her first, no flour, and let her fix where it starts and ends. Follow her decision even when it goes through the kitchen twice.
  2. She chooses what waits at the end and hides it herself, out of your sight.
  3. Print the prints. She presses the stamp, you sieve a little flour onto the sponge between presses.
  4. Make three arrow cards. She draws them, you tape them at Joseph's eye height rather than hers.
  5. Add two clues of her own. Ask what each is meant to tell him and write her answer on the back.
  6. Walk it once as a test, her leading and you playing Joseph. She will fix two things.
  7. Turn the lights down at six and hand him the flashlight at the door.

💡Write her clues down word for word. She will not remember the reasoning by Friday.

Day 32 · For the grown-up Who Came Past in the Night · Monday, February 1
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 7 months and sits solid with both hands free. Put him at the far end of the trail on a blanket with a wooden spoon and let Azlyn crawl toward him. He tracks her the whole way and laughs before she arrives. Keep him off the floured floor, and out in the frost hold his bare palm on a cold car roof for one second.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He goes in the stroller with a blanket over his legs and a hat over his ears. February wind at the top of a slide is a different thing at his height, so keep him low and moving. Five minutes on the baby swing and no more. He is passing things hand to hand now, so give him two rings for the walk home.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Evidence and inference, a big idea learnable at three.

A chewed leaf on the floor and a fox at the end of the hallway are different kinds of thing, and Azlyn spent the morning getting from one to the other. Scientists call the move inference: the leaf is what you can see, the fox is what you worked out. Three-year-olds do this better than the age suggests, as long as the evidence sits in front of them. Ask what does this tell us instead of who was it, and she has to say the middle step out loud. That middle step is the whole of science, and she will use it on you within a week.

⚠️

Safety: Flour on a hard floor is slippery in a way that puts adults down as fast as children. Sweep between rounds, keep it off tile and laminate near the stairs, and never lay a trail on a staircase. Sieve it rather than throwing it, so nobody breathes a cloud.

The Bird Menu

You need: paper · crayons · a saucer of seed, oats and raisins.

  1. Put the saucer in front of her and let her sort it. Seeds here, oats there, raisins in their own heap.
  2. Ask which a bird would go for first. Write her answer as a menu, one line per item, with her drawing of the bird beside it.
  3. Pin the menu on the window the feeders hang outside. She checks it against real birds all week.

What the Birds Take First

⏱️ 60 min🧰 6 items

You need: The four feeders from January 17, brought in off their branches (or 4 clean yogurt pots and string, if the wind took them), Warm soapy water, 1 dish brush and a cloth, 4 foods, a cup of each: sunflower seeds, mixed birdseed, oats and breadcrumbs, raisins, Masking tape and 1 marker, String, 1 ball, 1 tray

  1. Line the four feeders up on the table and tip what is left of each into its own saucer. She puts them in order, emptiest to fullest.
  2. She scrubs the pots in the warm soapy water and stands them on the tray. Sixteen days of birds leave a lot behind.
  3. Fill each pot with one food and one food only. She will want to mix them, and a mixed pot answers nothing.
  4. She draws a label for each one and you tape it on: a sunflower, a scatter of seed, a spoonful of oats, a raisin.
  5. Re-tie the strings and pull every knot tight. A pot that swings loose in a February wind empties itself in a day.
  6. Walk her past the menu she pinned on the window at 8:00 and ask which pot empties first. Write her answer on the menu.

💡She will want raisins in every pot, because raisins are the good one. Let her put them in the pot she thinks the birds like least, and the test still works.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

Hanging the Feeders

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Hang all four in new places this time, well apart, where she can see them from a window and a cat cannot reach. A clothesline, a bare branch, a hook under the eaves, a fence post. She picks every spot and you lift her to the high ones. February is the hard month out there, and four foods in four spots ask a better question than four in one.

Binoculars and the Bird Chart

Nothing will come to those feeders today. Birds take a day or two to find a feeder that has moved, so build her somewhere to sit and wait.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: Cardboard tubes, 4, 1 roll masking tape, Paper and crayons for the chart, Cushions and a blanket for the window seat, 1 pencil, The Groundhog Day note: February 2, when a woodchuck is said to come up and check on winter

  1. Tape two tubes side by side for her pair, and two more for yours. Nothing goes round her neck: she holds hers to her eyes with both hands.
  2. Let her color both pairs.
  3. Build the window seat: cushions under the window, blanket over her knees, chart and pencil beside her.
  4. Draw the chart with her. Five rows, one bird per row, a tick box at the end.
  5. Sit and watch. Ten minutes is a long time at three, so set the deal now: watch, something else, watch again.
  6. Tick nothing, and treat that as an answer. Ask why and write her reason at the bottom.
  7. Tell her what today is. February 2, Groundhog Day. Ask what she thinks the woodchuck saw.

💡Leave the chart on the windowsill with the pencil. She ticks it on Thursday when a chickadee turns up.

  • Draw birds out of a book instead.

🌳 Out again · pick one
  • Swimming
  • The quiet hour, if the after-school crowd is in

  • Straight home, if the morning ran long
Day 33 · For the grown-up Feeding the Birds · Tuesday, February 2
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 7 months and passes things from hand to hand all day. Give him a clean yogurt pot and a wooden spoon beside the table and let him swap them over. He bangs the two together inside ten minutes. The seed, the string and the raisins stay well out of reach.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He swims too if he is coming. At 7 months he sits supported in the water and slaps at it, and twenty minutes is enough before he goes cold. Hold him chest to chest for the first few minutes, so the echo and the shouting arrive with your face in front of him. Get him dry and dressed before you deal with yourself.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Delayed payoff is a muscle, and this is a gentle way to work it.

She filled four feeders this morning and no bird came this afternoon. That gap is the thing worth having. Waiting well builds through small waits with something visible at the end, and a feeder outside the window is the friendliest version. Nobody is asking her to sit still in front of a marshmallow. She hung it, she can see it, and the birds arrive on Thursday. Say out loud that they need a day or two to find it, so the wait carries a reason instead of an unexplained no. A three-year-old who waited and turned out right takes that with her.

⚠️

Safety: Old feeders carry droppings, so both pairs of hands get washed with soap after the scrubbing and again after the hanging, before anybody eats. Loose seed on the floor is choke-sized for a 7-month-old, so sweep before Kreston goes down. The string gets tied outside and the ball comes straight back indoors, because a loop of string at toddler height is a strangulation risk. The binoculars stay stringless for the same reason: no cord long enough to go over her head, on those or on anything else in the house. Swimming this afternoon. Both children stay within arm's reach in the water at all times, and no float or seat is a substitute for your hands.

Opening activity · 8:00–9:00 AM

The Winter Sleepers

You need: the Forest Family animals or any toys · 1 blanket · the sofa.

  1. Line the animals along the arm of the sofa. Ask which of them she thinks sleeps the whole winter.
  2. Hand her the four that do in this house's version: bear, groundhog, chipmunk, bat. Tuck them under a corner of the blanket together.
  3. Ask what a sleeping animal needs. Take her list as it comes, and tell her the cave gets built at 9:15.

Day 34 · The main event The Long Sleep · Wednesday, February 3
⏱️ 9:15 onward
🎨 MAKE
The main event · 9:15–10:15 AM

The Bear Cave

⏱️ 60 min🧰 6 items

You need: 1 large cardboard box, big enough for her to sit up in, Newspaper or scrap paper to tear for leaves, 1 blanket and 1 cushion, 1 roll masking tape, 1 flashlight, The Forest Family animals, or any toy animals

  1. Lay the box on its side with the opening facing away from the window. Run a hand round the inside for staples and tape over the ones you find.
  2. Tear the paper into leaves together. Fill a grocery bag and let the tearing run as long as she wants.
  3. Line the floor of the cave with the leaves, the blanket over them, and the cushion at the back wall.
  4. Tape a flap of card across part of the opening so the inside goes dark. She decides how much light gets in.
  5. Send her in with the flashlight and stay outside. Give her five clear minutes on her own before you ask a single question.
  6. Move the animals in one at a time, each to a spot she picks. Then get in with her, turn the flashlight off, and let the cave go dark.

💡Let her tear far more paper than the cave needs. Two hands pulling in opposite directions is work she can keep up for twenty minutes.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

Empty Nests in Bare Trees

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Nests show up in February and vanish again in April, so this is the month to look. Walk the road and the park with your eyes up and count the dark clumps in the bare branches. Some are nests, some are a knot of twigs. Find the highest and the lowest. Nobody is home in any of them, so say so.

Outdoors d34-outside.png
The Big Book of Little Days · January · Week 5Day 34 · main event →
Day 34 · Afternoon The Long Sleep · Wednesday, February 3
⏱️ 1:00 onward
🎨 MAKE
Second main event · 1:00–2:30 PM

Waking the Bears

The cave is dark and lined by lunchtime. Azlyn runs the afternoon on a wooden spoon and a pan lid, and winter ends whenever she says it does.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: The cave, 1 wooden spoon and 1 pan lid, 1 blanket each, 1 cup of warm milk and a snack, for eating inside, Books about bears or winter, 2–3, 1 flashlight

  1. Everybody hibernates. Into the cave or under a blanket, eyes shut, and hold it while you count to twenty out loud.
  2. Bang the pan lid once with the spoon. That is spring. Everybody wakes, stretches and comes out slow.
  3. Go round again with her holding the spoon. She decides how long winter lasts, three seconds the first time and two minutes the fourth.
  4. Change one rule each round. Sleep standing up. Sleep in a pile. Sleep with the flashlight on. Sleep and snore.
  5. Creep past a sleeping bear without waking it, then swap and let her creep past you. Getting caught is the fun of it, so get caught.
  6. Take the milk and the snack into the cave and eat in there with the flashlight on.
  7. Read the books in the cave and finish with everybody asleep and nobody banging anything.

💡Let her hold the pan lid for most of the rounds. Deciding when winter ends is a lot of power for a three-year-old.

Day 34 · For the grown-up The Long Sleep · Wednesday, February 3
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 7 months. Sit him at the cave mouth propped on a cushion with you beside him, and let Azlyn crawl in and out past him. The light drops as she goes in and comes back as she comes out, and he turns his head after it. Give him a big sheet of paper to crush in both hands.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

Sit him in the board-book corner at the library while Azlyn chooses. At 7 months he mouths every book he gets hold of, and he holds one in each hand and swaps them. Let Azlyn pick his and carry it to the desk. At home the pan lid stays well away from his ears.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Pretending to sleep is real self-regulation practice.

Azlyn lying still with her eyes shut while you count to twenty is doing something hard on purpose. She wants to move, she knows the rule, and she holds herself to it anyway. Researchers call that inhibitory control, and games with a stop-and-go rule build it better than being told to sit still, because the rule belongs to the game. The round where she holds the pan lid works harder: running the stop and the go for somebody else takes more control than following it. Freeze games, musical statues and sleeping lions sit in the same family. Reach for one on the afternoons she is climbing the walls.

⚠️

Safety: Kreston is 7 months and cannot get himself out of anywhere. He goes in the cave only with you in it, and never on his own for a second. Torn paper and loose blankets stay clear of his face. Check the box for staples before either of them climbs in, and tape over every one you find.

Opening activity · 8:00–9:00 AM

Guess the Shadow

You need: 1 flashlight · a pale wall · 3 toy animals · your hands.

  1. Turn the big light off, sit her facing the wall, and hold the flashlight behind your shoulder.
  2. Put one animal in the beam. Ask which one it is before she turns round.
  3. Move it closer to the flashlight and let the shadow swell. Hand her the flashlight until 9:15.

Day 35 · The main event The Shadow Forest · Thursday, February 4
⏱️ 9:15 onward
🎨 MAKE
The main event · 9:15–10:15 AM

The Shadow Animals

⏱️ 60 min🧰 6 items

You need: Cereal boxes or thick card, 4–5, Scissors (adult), Craft sticks, straws or pencils, 1 roll masking tape, 1 flashlight, A pale wall or a white door

  1. Draw the four animals on the cereal box: fox, owl, deer, raccoon. Big simple outlines, no detail inside. You draw, she directs.
  2. Cut them out. Card this thick is adult work: she holds the box flat while you cut.
  3. Tape a craft stick low on the back of each, so her hand stays out of the beam.
  4. Test the first one against the wall. If the ears are too small or the legs have joined into a block, cut wider and test again.
  5. Do the same to all four. Deer antlers have to be fat, and an owl needs a notch between its ear tufts.
  6. Line them up and test from across the room. Any animal she cannot name goes back for cutting.

💡Cut everything fatter than looks right. Thin legs and fine antlers vanish on the wall.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

The Longest Shadow

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Stop at the feeders on the way out. The sunflower seeds have gone down, and a chickadee comes back for more if you hold still. Let her tick the chart when you get in. The sun stays low all day in early February, so shadows run long. Stand her on the sidewalk at eleven, draw round her shadow in chalk, and pace it out in her steps. Come back past the chalk mark on the way home.

🎨 MAKE
Second main event · 1:00–2:30 PM

The Puppet Show Behind the Sheet

A sheet clipped across a doorway turns the week into something she can perform. She has four animals, one flashlight, and an audience.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: 1 white or pale sheet, Clothespins or binder clips, 6, A doorway, or 2 dining chairs back to back, 1 flashlight, The shadow puppets, Paper and crayons for tickets and a poster

  1. Clip the sheet across the doorway, pulled tight, floor to above her head. Two chairs back to back work if clips will not hold.
  2. Stand the flashlight behind the sheet on the floor or a low stool, aimed at the middle.
  3. Test the distance. Close to the sheet the fox is small and sharp; back near the flashlight he is huge and soft.
  4. Make the poster and the tickets. She draws, you write the words she dictates.
  5. Sit the audience down: Kreston propped on cushions, teddies either side, whoever else is home.
  6. She tells the week back through the puppets: coats on Friday, the tree on Saturday, somebody past in the night on Monday. Give her the day and she supplies the rest.
  7. Swap sides at the end. You run the fox, and the last five minutes go with the flashlight off.

💡Move the flashlight back further than feels right. A flashlight against the sheet gives one bright spot and four tiny animals.

Day 35 · For the grown-up The Shadow Forest · Thursday, February 4
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 7 months. Lay him on his back and hold the flashlight above him off to one side, your hand between the beam and his face. Move your fingers through it. He follows the shape across the ceiling, loses it, finds it again. Outside, park him with the low sun behind him and wave from a few feet back.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

The garden center is warm and bright, so sit him on your lap for ten minutes. Hold a big leaf out to one side, where he has to reach across himself. At 7 months that cross-body reach is new work. At the show he sits in the front row, and moving shapes on a lit sheet hold him longer than a book.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Shadows are confusing at three, and the confusion is worth exploring.

Ask Azlyn what a shadow is made of and you get real thought in the answer and no truth in it. Three-year-olds treat a shadow as a thing that belongs to an object and travels with it, rather than as blocked light. The real version takes a couple of years of flashlight time. Every test today feeds that version: close to the sheet, back near the flashlight, one hand in the beam. Hold off on the tidy explanation. Give her the flashlight, let her run the tests, and answer the questions she asks rather than the ones she has not reached.

⚠️

Safety: Loose craft sticks and straws stay off the floor while Kreston is down. They splinter, and they fit down his throat, so count them onto the table and back off it. Card this thick is yours to cut and the scissors stay with you. Clip the sheet where it can come down without bringing anything with it, a door frame rather than a curtain pole or a shelf. Stand the flashlight on the floor instead of a stack of books, and with the room lights off keep Kreston inside arm's reach the whole time.
